speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, June 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes to conclude my remarks which I began last evening.
I had indicated that during the past number of years, approximately since 1962 which is about the time capital punishment was abolished in this country in fact if not in law, there has been an increase in the murder rate in Canada of some 150 per cent. I think those who argue that this is not significant do so on the basis that there has been an increase of a similar proportion in other violent crimes. It seems to me, however, that we have a situation in which the general application of law in this country has been of an excessively permissive nature. We have a peculiar situation where the federal government takes the position that it does not want to enforce its own laws.
When the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) piloted the last bill through this House some three years ago, he quite plainly indicated during that debate that he was retaining capital punishment for murderers of policemen and prison guards simply as a conciliatory move toward policemen and prison guards while indicating at the same time that he did not have the slightest intention of applying that law. I think the result of that kind of attitude on the part of a solicitor general is that it sets a bad example. It indicates that he does not have the desire or the backbone to apply the law as it stands, that he is chicken and, finally, I think the most drastic result is that it creates a situation in which there develops a disrespect for the law. People do not believe that the law will be applied and ask why they should pay attention to it, particularly when they consider the position taken by the Solicitor General.
Three or four years ago I had the interesting experience of visiting the Isle of Man and talking to the attorney general there. You may recall, sir, that the Isle of Man is one of the few places in the world that retains corporal punishment as well. Perhaps to come to grips with the
argument that even though the number of murders has increased the number of other violent crimes has increased as well, it might be useful to try to correlate that with the abolition of corporal punishment. In conversations, the attorney general of the Isle of Man suggested to me that because they still use corporal punishment for violent crimes such as assaults, rapes and things of that nature, the incidence of those kinds of crime is substantially less on that island than it is any place where corporal punishment was abandoned a long time ago. Perhaps there is reason to give consideration to the whole question or permissiveness and the reapplication of some of those former methods of dealing with various types of crime.
I think it has been shown during the course of this debate that statistics concerning whether capital punishment is a deterrent or not, are not very helpful. Those who speak in favour of abolition provide backup statistics showing that the murder rate in abolitionist countries is no higher and possibly even is less than that in countries where capital punishment is retained. Those who favour the retention of capital punishment have provided statistics showing that the murder rate is lower in countries where capital punishment is retained. The statistics therefore are not very helpful in that people select statistics which are useful to substantiate their position. Unfortunately, statistics for other countries do not apply to Canada. One cannot determine if capital punishment alone affects the murder rate in a country; one must consider a host of other cultural and economic factors as well. Perhaps we can draw important conclusions from an examination of statistics applying to other countries, but only an examination of relevant Canadian statistics will allow us to come to valid conclusions about conditions in Canada. As I said, the present murder rate is 2.4 per cent per 100,000 of population; before 1960 it was 1.2 per cent. One could argue that the partial abolition of the death sentence has brought about a 150 per cent increase in the murder rate.
[DOT] (mo)
To determine if capital punishment is a deterrent, I suggest we should reinstate capital punishment for a five-year period, with a view to studying if the murder rate comes down again. If such a study were carried out under scientific conditions in one country, it would, perhaps, give us the most accurate reading of the effects of capital punishment. I also wish to call attention to the cost of incarcerating a man. We are told that it costs about $18,000 per year to keep one person in prison; therefore, keeping someone in prison for 25 years would cost about $.5 million. The question is, should the taxpayer shoulder that kind of burden?
Another point to which I referred last evening has to do with the hanging of an innocent person. According to statistics I have seen, there has been only one such case in this country in recent memory; on the other hand, there

have been seven repeat murders, that is to say, murders committed by convicted murderers who have been released for some reason or who were out on parole. Therefore, the ratio of deaths inflicted on innocent people to deaths inflicted by repeat murderers is seven to one. From cold statistics it is clear that fewer innocent people will die if murderers are hanged that if they are not hanged.
I am about to make a suggestion which will make judges and juries shudder. The law requires juries to be certain beyond any reasonable doubt about the guilt of the accused before convicting. I suggest that judges and juries should be given some added responsibility in cases where a mistake is made and an innocent person hangs. Perhaps we should devise methods for making judges and juries accountable for their decisions. Such provision, perhaps, would lessen further the possibility of innocent persons being hanged.
We must consider the question of the responsibility of members of parliament to their constituents. Without question, the primary responsibility of the member is to represent in this House those who elected him. The member of parliament is the spokesman for, perhaps, 100,000 constituents; he speaks on their behalf in this House. I do not wish to belittle those hon. members who say that they will vote on any issues in accordance with their consciences, but I say that while it is the member's responsibility to exercise his judgment, at the same time he must keep in mind the stated desires of his constituents if it is possible to determine those desires clearly. I suggest that with regard to the particular issue we are debating at present, the desires of constituents are clearly known.
As I said, I suggest that we should introduce again for a five-year trial period. Capital punishment for capital murder. Only that way can we determine accurately the effects of capital punishment and see whether, in the context of our social and economic conditions, it is a deterrent in Canada. We might consider allowing the prisoner to choose whether he will be in prison for 25 years or executed. Since we live in a democracy, we might consider such an idea. It might require amending the legislation, to give the prisoner that choice. I say this as many feel that a 25-year prison term is more cruel than capital punishment. I do not think anyone should make the decisions for another person. Only the convicted murderer should be allowed to make that choice. Such provision would require an amendment to the legislation now before the House.
We must also consider whether people feel the law provides enough protection. Some feel that if murderers were hanged for capital murder society would be more effectively protected. Surely, the imposition of capital punishment shows emphatically that society abhors murder. Capital punishment emphasizes society's total rejection, total abhorrence of the cold-blooded, calculated killing of another person, without just cause.
Finally, I conclude by suggesting that this debate, at best, will only provide an interim solution to the problem of how we are to treat murderers. In the final analysis we must consider ways of prevention. Neither imprisonment for 25 years nor hanging will stop murders being committed. We must dedicate ourselves to undertaking intensive research programs to determine why people commit murder. What factors shape personalities; what personality
[Mr. Yewchuk.l
traits lead to the commission of murder? Once we know why certain people tend to commit murder, we may be in a position to bring in ultimate solutions which will prevent the occurrence of murder. In the long run that must be the aim. In my view this bill, at best, will deal with the problem only in the short term.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for those who believe that human life is a value in itself, that in the most literal sense it is a precondition for all other value systems, it must be obvious that the issue of capital punishment is, from a moral perspective, probably the most important issue on which a politician is asked to make a judgment.
By this I mean that before one can debate the morality of any social or political system, liberalism, socialism or conservatism, one must assume at the outset that all mankind has a preceding moral right to exist, that all men have an equal claim at the outset, once they are born, to continue to exist. It is for this reason that I believe most seriously that those who favour capital punishment have upon themselves the moral onus to prove that this form of killing by the state is justified. It may turn out that their case can be persuasive, but it cannot be denied that it is up to them to establish their case. That is the crucial moral consideration, because what is involved in the debate on capital punishment is the right of the state to kill. It has to be put as bluntly as that. Those who are arguing for capital punishment have to present to us a moral argument for the right to kill a human being.
I believe that based on this fundamental assumption, the deliberate taking of a human life is warranted in only two kinds of situations, both of which rest on a common assumption. The first is self defence by an individual. If a man, woman or child is attacked by another human being, in my view that person has the right, in order to protect his or her life, to kill, if necessary, the attacker. The second circumstance in which I believe it is morally appropriate for killing to take place is when one nation or state declares war or, even without declaration, invades another state with the purpose of imposing upon that second state their rule by force, violence and killing. Under those circumstances also I believe it is right and morally justified, horrible as it is, to kill. That is collectively those members of a state have the right to defend themselves against others.
The two points, as I say, really are identical in principle. One is the right of an individual to protect his or her life from a violent threat upon it. The other is the collective right of a state or collection of individuals to do the same.
I have not been persuaded that there is any other situation which justifies the killing of another human being. In short, I am not persuaded that capital punishment can be supported by reason or moral argument. I have not, of course, been here for the full debate that has taken place in this House, but I have consulted the arguments put forward by both sides of this issue by all members.
I want to make it clear at the outset that I am not questioning the integrity of those who have reached a decision that is different from my own. I am questioning
June 15, 1976

the reasoning, the moral reasoning in particular, which has led to the conclusion reached by those who favour capital punishment.
What are the arguments that have been put forward by the retentionists in favour of capital punishment? I repeat, morally it is up to the retentionists to prove their case for the right of the state to kill another human being. There are three arguments that have been presented and I would like to discuss them.
The first argument comes in two forms. It is that the majority of Canadians want capital punishment. Another variant of the same argument is "the majority of my constituents want capital punishment". Many members have argued that they have an obligation to vote for capital punishment because a Gallup poll survey of the nation indicates that most Canadians or most of their constituents favour capital punishment.
The acceptance of this argument largely depends, in fact entirely depends, on the acceptance of the view that democratic government rests simply on the notion of head counting. In my opinion, this view is erroneous both as a general theory of democracy and as one which holds in particular for representative democracy. The great democrats in the whole history of democratic government from Pericles in ancient Greece to John Stuart Mill, the great democrat of the nineteenth century, have always argued that discussion based on reason and evidence is an essential aspect of democratic decision making. When the community is small enough, it is possible for everyone who is affected by a law to actually make the law. That was possible in the model of the traditional Greek city state or in the early communities established in North America. In little villages, it was possible for all those affected by the laws of those communities to take part in open debate, to listen to the pros and cons, the evidence for or against a particular motion. They could be present for the debate. The argument makes sense in that context.
However, rational discussion in which all the citizens can hear the arguments and consider the evidence is impossible in a large democratic state like Canada. This is why in the last century representative democracy came into being for the first time. In this instance, the instance of representative democracy, it is those who are elected by the people who have the obligation to consider basic principles, listen to each other in debate and consult the evidence that is to be found both within their own country and abroad. Our constituents do not have the time to weigh the evidence and consider the arguments. They are preoccupied on a day-to-day basis with earning their livelihood. That is their serious, immediate and pressing concern. They do not have the opportunity that we in this chamber have to look at the evidence and listen to each other in order to formulate a final opinion. We, therefore, must make the decision. As elected members of parliament, we must take the consequences, not only on capital punishment, but on all other issues.
The point I am making does not merely hold for capital punishment. It holds for all law-making in a democratic society. This is so fundamental to the notion of representative democracy that, frankly, I have been somewhat amazed by a number of members of parliament arguing the contrary case, namely that you can simply go to your
Capital Punishment
constituency and count heads or get a public opinion poll survey from the country as a whole. In my view, the argument that a member of parliament must simply respond in a direct way in opinion surveys or head counts is not merely wrong; it is anti-democratic. It denies that other crucial element in democracy, namely that decisions are to be reached after reasonable discussion, hours of persuasion and the thorough consideration of evidence. All of these must have their day.

speechtext:
If that is the case, I want to consider the two arguments which have been put forward to justify capital punishment and which could be used to influence members on either side who are prepared to exercise their responsibility to reach a decision. The first argument goes as follows: the punishment must fit the crime, and the supreme crime merits the supreme punishment. From the point of view of criminology I accept the principle involved-the more severe the crime, the more severe the punishment. I think that is proper. I think that is just. The idea embodied in this principle is to be found in the very bill we are considering: there is a distinction made between first degree and second degree murder; there is a distinction made in the length of sentence imposed; there is also a distinction between the severity of sentencing a man or a woman for murder and sentencing a person for a lesser crime. So I accept the principle that the punishment must correspond in some sense to the severity of the crime, and repeat that it is embodied in the bill which is before the House. That is not the issue, however.
The issue for those who argue in favour of capital punishment demands a positive answer to the following question: does murder by an individual require murder by the state? Is that the conclusion one must reach after accepting the general principle that punishment must correspond with the crime in degree of severity? I conclude that those who say that murder requires capital punishment as a form of justice are erroneous in their reasoning and I should like to make the case in the following way.
If a group of men or women are involved in a brawl and some of them are severely injured in that brawl, perhaps permanently maimed, we do not under our judicial system in the middle of the 20th Century say that the state must set about imposing a similar kind of physical violence on those who perpetrated the wrongdoing. If a man breaks another man's leg, deliberately and callously, the state does not say that the guilty person must be taken to jail and have his leg broken in a corresponding fashion. It is essential we recognize this to be the case. Those who are arguing in favour of capital punishment make the same

June 15, 1976
Capital Punishment
kind of serious mistake in their moral reasoning when they conclude that a murder by an individual calls for a corresponding murder by the state. I am sure they would not argue that if a man breaks another man's leg the state has an obligation to break his leg. To my mind, the same idea is involved in the two instances. So, if it is acknowledged that severe punishment is required, this does not lead to the conclusion that a heinous murder must in justice require an equally violent death imposed by the state or the person who committed the first act.
Now, I turn to what is, at least for me, the only serious argument which could be advanced in favour of capital punishment if it were well-founded on evidence, that is, the argument that execution is a deterrent. If those who have argued for capital punishment could bring before the House, either in terms of the Canadian experience or the experience abroad, substantial evidence that capital punishment, horrible as it is to my mind, is a significant deterrent to murder I would be prepared to give the matter serious consideration.
But what is the evidence? I shall not trot out the statistics; they have already been presented by members of all parties and, in particular, by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). I want to pay tribute to the Solicitor General for the outstanding job he has done in presenting the moral issue. The Solicitor General and others have shown that the evidence-and I shall not put it stronger than this-is simply not persuasive. One can look at other countries-I am thinking particularly of the United States-and reach conflicting conclusions. Some of the evidence would lead to the conclusion that capital punishment is, indeed, effective as a deterrent. But this is only so long as one does not look at the position in a neighbouring state in the United States, for instance, or in a country in western Europe, at which point one finds that the removal of capital punishment has not led to more cases of capital crime. In my judgment, the evidence is, on balance, more strongly on the side that capital punishment is not a deterrent, though I am prepared to concede to those who argue in favour of capital punishment that it is not absolutely clear whether it is a deterrent or not.
Now I come back to my first comments. If it is not clear that it is a deterrent, and if we are by no means certain that the brutal killing of a human being can be justified on moral grounds, how else can we reasonably reach the conclusion that capital punishment is permissible? After all, capital punishment is undeniably brutal; we put a noose around a person's neck and let him drop, and hang, and die. The issue has to be seen as seriously and as intensely as that. If the evidence is not overwhelmingly persuasive that we are likely to head off murders, what moral justification do we have as human beings to kill another human being? I say we have no such justification and therefore I conclude that the deterrent argument, in the face of this moral reasoning, is not an acceptable one.
I draw a further conclusion, Mr. Speaker. If we do not accept capital punishment as a form of primitive justice, and if we do not accept it as a deterrent, then how can we accept it? To those who approve the reasoning on those two points and still insist on capital punishment I would say, as did the great French author and playwright, Albert Camus, that the only justification which is left, the only

psychological motive which is left, is the latent, emotional hangover of vengeance. We cannot base any law in Canada on the notion of vengeance.
[DOT] (U40)
This bill does recognize the seriousness of murder. Those of us who argue against capital punishment would also argue with the same degree of seriousness and concern against any act of murder. Sometimes those who take a contrary position suggest that those of us who are abolitionists are somehow soft on crime or indifferent to human cruelty. I think just the contrary is the case: those of us who are determined abolitionists I suggest are equally determined in our opposition to violence in society as a whole, quite apart from the issue of capital punishment. We have concern for the victims of crime, very much so. What we want is to change society as much as we possibly can to remove the causes of murder and other forms of violence. I for one do not claim to have all the answers to violent murder. But this is where the real effort must be made in the years ahead.
Recognizing the moral wrongness of murder, we support the view that there has to be severe punishment to make it clear that our society does not condone that kind of behaviour. I suggest that the distinction in this bill between first degree and second degree murder does precisely that. It makes a distinction between the motive for and cause of the different kinds of murder. In my view, the punishment imposed for either degree of murder is sufficient to deter anyone in the land from contemplating in a cold-blooded way an act of murder, if that person is the kind who will be deterred at all. We do not need capital punishment as a further deterrent.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I urge all members of this House in particular to reject what I regard as the terribly irresponsible argument that in a democracy we are required simply to count heads, whether in the nation or in our constituencies. That surely cannot be justification for voting either for or against capital punishment. I ask all members to consider very carefully whether we want to have a system that perpetuates the doctrine of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth and have the state indulge in cold-blooded violence as a reciprocal act against any man or woman who has murdered someone else in society-an argument that I reject.
Alternatively, Mr. Speaker, I ask them to consider dispassionately and with reason the evidence on the question of deterrence. I suggest to those members who are still wavering, particularly on the deterrence argument- because I think that is crucial-to consider this, that if the evidence at best is ambiguous, if at best it is not clear or totally persuasive, then they have a moral obligation in this debate to come down on the side of life, on the side of those who oppose capital punishment.

Mr. Speaker, with the indulgence of the House it is my intention to take a few moments to express my point of view on this very important matter. I do so not with the expectation that anything I say will change one iota the view of any other member. The length of this debate alone has indicated the importance that members attach to it. After all, there is a very heavy responsibility on all of us to try to come up with
June 15, 1976

what is the most logical and sound decision on this legislation. I feel, too, that I have a responsibility to the people I represent; they should know not only how I vote on a matter such as this, but why I do so.
I say at once that the sincerity of no member can be questioned, regardless how he votes on this bill or what his views may be. This is a subject on which all members of the House have done a great deal of soul searching. We have, in a sense, held in the balance at the present time the lives of certain people, not only those on death row but those of our citizens who may commit murder in the future. As far as those on death row at the moment are concerned, I think there might be justification for making them exempt from the provisions of this bill. That fact might sway some members from voting as they otherwise might do.
I want to say at once, Mr. Speaker, that I am going to vote against this bill. We are, of course, concerned, regardless which side of the argument we are on, with the sanctity of human life. I think that our differences stem not from that but from the way we interpret it. The leader of the New Democratic Party who spoke a few moments ago I think debased the language by equating capital punishment with murder. I think that the two things are entirely different. The end result is the same in that a life is terminated, but under entirely different circumstances.
Murder results when someone, who may be the best citizen possible, who walks uprightly in the eyes of his fellow citizens and in the eyes of God, has his life taken away by another person under conditions over which he has no direct control. No person in this country need ever be hanged, regardless what the law provides; all he need do is not murder anybody. Our law takes every precaution to see that no one in this country is ever unjustly accused or convicted, but after the due process of law is carried out I find it difficult to understand why people cannot bring themselves to approve of capital punishment because they claim to have a reverence for life. Yet large numbers of those same people in many cases have approved abortion on demand. To me that is a much worse act on the part of society. In the one case you are taking the life of an individual who has had his chance and who could have lived his life in a way that society would approve rather than have to condemn. On the other hand, you are taking a life which has never had a chance, a life entirely before the individual. I find this a contradictory kind of thinking.
Much has been said as to whether capital punishment or the lack of it is a deterrent to crime. I think it is not an immediate deterrent either way. A potential murderer does not suddenly change his mind at that very instant and commit a murder. Therefore, even if we can devise a law that is a real deterrent it will have little or no deterrent effect on the hardened criminal or on the person who is so callous toward the right of other people to life that he does not hesitate to take someone's life if that is convenient. Any deterrent effect will not become evident for a generation at least, because the important point in life when our character's are formulated is when we are very young. I believe that as a twig is bent, so is the tree inclined. I get a little tired of people trying to reform hardened criminals. Once they have become hardened and have been through
Capital Punishment
the legal process and are in a penitentiary for years, in some cases, then in most cases it is already far too late.
What society has to do is impress on the people in the days of their youth and their childhood that there are certain things society will not allow and will not tolerate. It is our belief as civilized people that each one of us has the inalienable right to life, and if someone takes it upon himself to take away that right unjustly society will not accept that kind of behaviour. It is abhorrent to society. We must impress upon all our people that there are certain things which are just not tolerable by society, and one of them is cold-blooded, planned and deliberate murder. This is something society will not accept. Therefore, to make society's attitude with regard to that kind of behaviour abundantly clear society should in my judgment decide that anyone who plans in cold blood to take someone else's life should forfeit his own.
In addition there are other categories of behaviour which deserve and warrant capital punishment. Treason under certain circumstances is one. We should not eliminate the possibility of capital punishment for treason. Mass killing, such as putting bombs on aircraft in order to collect the insurance on someone, or for some other equally abhorrent reason, is such callous and outrageous behaviours that anyone who contemplates that kind of conduct should know in advance that if he carries it out he will pay the supreme penalty of capital punishment.
Those are some of the reasons I feel capital punishment should not be completely eliminated. I am not entirely satisfied with the interim law, the life of which is five years and which will not expire for another year and a half, but I think it is better law than the law represented in this bill. Therefore, I will vote against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that very few if any of us consciously contemplated, when we decided to run for public office, that we would find ourselves playing a decisive role in the resolution of a question as awesome as that of life or death. Yet, here we are, with all our individual limitations, required by the office we hold to make a decision on as profoundly an important issue as has ever divided responsible Canadians.
It is not open to anyone among us to take refuge in the comforting illusion that we are debating nothing more than an abstract theory of criminal justice, and that it will be the Cabinet's sole responsibility to decide the actual fate of individual murderers if this bill is defeated. I want to make it very clear that, if a majority of hon. members vote against abolition, some people are going to be hanged. Their death would be a direct consequence of the negative decision made by this House on this bill.

I say that, Mr. Speaker, not from any desire to be morbid or melodramatic, nor from any desire to try to absolve the cabinet, in advance, of its share of responsibility for the taking of human life in the future, if this bill is defeated. I say it in order to impress upon the House as strongly as I can that what we will actually be deciding, when we vote on this bill, is not merely how the law of the land will be written, but also whether some human beings will live or die.

Capital Punishment
At this moment, eleven men are being held in Canadian prisons under sentence of death for the murder of policemen or prison officials. Some have exhausted their rights of appeal. Others have not. Therefore, while it is impossible to pre-judge how cabinet will treat any individual case when the time comes to decide whether to invoke the royal prerogative of mercy and commute a death sentence to life imprisonment, it is inevitable that the defeat of this bill would eventually place the hangman's noose around some person's neck. To make that quite clear: if this bill is defeated, some people will certainly hang. While members are free to vote as they wish, those who vote against the bill, for whatever reason, cannot escape their personal share of responsibility for the hangings which will take place if the bill is defeated.
It is in that context, Mr. Speaker, that I wish to place my remarks on the issue before us. Any discussion of capital punishment must begin with the identification of its intended purpose, which is clearly the security of society, the protection of innocent people against the ultimate criminal violence. It is not that goal which divides us. It is a goal we all share. What divides us is the question of the appropriateness of state execution of murderers as a means of achieving that goal.
It is clear that the protection of innocent people against assaults on their lives and liberty is one of the highest duties of the state. It is equally clear that this duty requires the aggressive and effective prevention, prosecution and punishment of criminal violence. It is essential that people have confidence in the law, essential that they have confidence in the ability of the legal process to protect them against the lawless. Reinforcing that vital sense of confidence and security is the primary aim of Bill C-83, the companion piece to the bill we are now debating.
Longer mandatory sentence and the tightening of parole regulations in relation to convicted murderers will give society the assurance it needs that those who have unlawfully taken the life of another will be removed from our midst for a very long time. Other provisions are designed to restrict the availability of guns, the most common murder weapons, and to strenghten the ability of our police forces to prevent and solve crimes.
There is every reason to believe that such measures will effectively inhibit criminal activity, whereas capital punishment offers no such assurance. That is why the time has come for Parliament to decide whether we should remove capital punishment from the Criminal Code. The crux of the question before us is whether execution is an effective and therefore justifiable weapon for the state to use in order to deter potential murderers.
There are those who sincerely believe that no man or group of men ever have the right to end a human life. They believe that life is a divine gift which only God has the right to take away. I am not one of those who share that belief. Our law, from its earliest beginnings, has always recognized the rights of an individual to kill another when there exist reasonable grounds for believing that killing an aggressor is necessary to the protection of one's own life or that of another. Moral philosophers and theologians have recognized for many centuries the right of a country to

defend itself in a just war, even when such defence involves the killing of enemies.

So the question before us is not whether execution by the state is justifiable per se, in itself. The question is whether state execution is an effective deterrent to murder, and therefore a justifiable act of collective self-defence.
The deterrent effect of capital punishment is at the very core of the issue, and since one's moral view of the justification of capital punishment is entirely determined by one's judgment of its deterrent effect, the proper focus of this debate is factual data and logical induction, not moral philosophy. In that sense, the issue before us must be resolved by a practical rather than a moral judgment.
I repeat my argumentation. Unless you are of a certain sect, or if you are a conscientious objector, in a moral sense the act of killing can be permissible in certain circumstances, like self-defence. Therefore, you have to make the practical judgment if, in a precise case, you are actually engaged in self-defence or vengeance. That, I think, is a practical judgment. Is it a good way for society to defend itself to hang people? I know there are those who say execution is justified because it prevents a murderer from ever again committing the same crime. It certainly does. If you hang a man, he will not go and shoot anyone else. But if you rely on that kind of reasoning, you are killing a man, not because his death may deter others from following in his footsteps but because of what he might possibly do at some future time. To justify such a preventive execution there would have to be some reasonable grounds for believing that a convicted murderer, if released into society- and, as we are seeking in Bill C-83, after a very long period of time-would murder again. In fact, the probability lies strongly in the other direction.
We know of only four people who have been found guilty of murder by a Canadian court, and convicted of murder a second time. In order to be absolutely sure that no murderer would murder again, we would have to take the lives of all persons convicted of either first or second degree murder, even though the probability is that an infinitesimal percentage of them would ever commit murder again if allowed to live. To me, that is an unacceptably high price to pay in human lives for a sense of security insignificantly greater than we have now. I might ask those who would execute a person to prevent a future murder how they could logically avoid advocating the execution of mentally-ill people who are found to have homicidal tendencies? You may say, "Let's execute the murderer for the crime he has committed. Let's take a life for a life. Let's remove a savage animal from the human race." I do not deny that society has the right to punish a criminal and the right to make the punishment fit the crime, but to kill a man for punishment alone is an act of revenge-nothing else. Some would prefer to call it retribution because that word has a nicer sound. But the meaning is the same.
Are we, as a society, so lacking in respect for ourselves, so lacking in hope for human betterment, so socially bankrupt that we are ready to accept state vengeance as our penal philosophy? Mr. Speaker, I think I have some understanding of the feelings here because I have received correspondence from relatives or friends of murdered people. I
June 15, 1976

understand individuals who fight back at the murderer of a loved one and kill him in a frenzy of passionate grief. I understand that they sometimes have been excused by the courts because they were thought to have temporarily lost control of their reason. I repeat that I have received letters and telegrams from relatives or friends of murdered people. I have been deeply moved by them and am deeply sympathetic to the suffering of those who endured such a tragedy and cruel loss of a loved one.
But the state cannot claim the excuse of blind grief or unreasoning passion. Long after the provocative act, long after calm and deliberate consideration, long after time for assessment and time to cool off and assemble its reason, the state cannot claim that justification when it kills a man. It should be understood that my primary concern here is not compassion for the murderer. My concern is for the society which adopts vengeance as an acceptable motive for its collective behaviour. If we make that choice, we will snuff out some of that boundless hope and confidence in ourselves and other people which has marked our maturing as a free people.
We will have chosen violence as a weapon against the violence we profess to abhor. Who is so confident that he knows for sure that such an official endorsement of violence will not harden the society we were elected to improve, will not pervade gradually many different relationships in our society? Who is so confident that he knows for sure that acceptance of state violence will not lead to the greater social acceptance of lesser forms of violence among our people? Vengeance and violence damage and destroy those who adopt them, and lessen respect for the dignity and rights of others among those who condone them.
There is only one other possible justification for capital punishment-the one we started with-the belief that execution of murderers will protect society by acting as a deterrent to the commission of murder by other people. There are some who adopt an experimental approach to the question of deterrence, like a scientist experimenting with different combinations of chemicals in the search for a new healing drug. "Let us try it," they say, "and see if it works. If it does, we will keep it. If it does not, we can always stop using it. Let us not slam the door, "they say," on a possibly effective weapon against murder," on some specious philosophical grounds." There are innocent lives at stake. If capital punishment prevents just one murder," they say, "it will be adequately justified."
That is compelling rhetoric, but it contains a fatal flaw, namely, that we would be experimenting with human lives. Respect for human life is absolutely vital to the rights and freedom we all enjoy. Even the life of the most hardened criminal must be accorded some degree of respect in a free society. If we take that life without proven purpose, without proven necessity, then we weaken dangerously one of the fundamental principles which allow us to live together in peace, harmony and mutual respect.

Capital Punishment

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: That is why free peoples have always insisted that the onus is on the person who would interfere with another's life or liberty to prove that such interference is necessary for the common good. Strictly speaking, therefore, it is not up to me, as an abolitionist, to prove that the execution of murderers will not prevent other murders. It is up to the advocates of capital punishment to prove that it will. If they cannot, their case must fail.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Otherwise, this debate turns into a guessing game and the lives of human beings become so many chips on the poker table. That is not good enough. I do not want to hear your guesses about the deterrent value of capital punishment. I do not want to hear about gut feelings. I want proof. Not absolute proof. Not even proof beyond a reasonable doubt. A preponderance of evidence will do. A preponderance of available evidence showing that executions are likely to deter other murders would serve as an adequate justification for the act, an adequate guarantee that a human life was not being taken capriciously.
Show me the evidence that capital punishment anywhere, at any time, has deterred other people from committing murder. My own reading of the speeches made here on this issue since the first week of May, together with the Solicitor General's (Mr. Allmand) daily monitoring of the debate, have indicated that no such evidence has been placed before the House. The evidence does not exist, either in the Canadian experience or in the experience of any other jurisdiction. At best-and I realize that statistics have been put forward on both sides-the statistics are inconclusive. They prove nothing. They prove there is doubt. There is no evidence proving that the use or non-use of capital punishment has had any effect whatsoever on murder rates anywhere in the world.
I must confess I cannot understand why anyone would agree to kill a man without the least shred of assurance that his death would accomplish any worth-while social purpose. If penalties applied by the state against lawbreakers cannot be justified for their rehabilitative, punitive or deterrent value, they cannot be justified at all-not in a civilized society. Capital punishment fails on all three counts. To retain it in the Criminal Code of Canada would be to abandon reason in favour of vengeance; to abandon hope and confidence in favour of a despairing acceptance of our inability to cope with violent crime except with violence.
It is because I have an enduring confidence in mankind, and confidence in society's ability to protect itself without taking human life, that I am eager to support this bill and vote for the abolition of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add a few words in the debate on Bill C-84 to abolish capital punishment in Canada. There have been many speakers on both sides of this question. There have been speakers who have quoted the scriptures, logic, philosophers, learned judges, statistics, psychiatrists, historians and sociologists to support their particular point of view. I do not intend to use those disciplines in any depth
June 15, 1976

Capital Punishment
in the comments which I wish to make today. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his remarks made reference to letters which he had received from the families of victims who have been murdered. That is the particular point that I want to talk about today. He said he had a great deal of feeling, compassion and understanding for them. I suppose each of us who takes part in this debate is to some extent ruled and governed by, and our logic is oriented around, the experiences we have had in life. I want to speak from the point of view of the family and close friends of the victims of murder, for they are equally victims with the persons who lost their lives because of a crime of violence.
I know, personally, people who have lost a member of their family to a murderer. In the main, the family and the friends are lost to society, sometimes forever. There is no society, group, agency or government which really cares for those who have lost a member of their family to a murderer. Many of these people never make it back into the mainstream of society. They are lost, empty and sad. There is a sadness about them that many of us cannot comprehend. Some become bitter and withdraw from society because in their view there is no justice. The accused is tried, found guilty and sentenced to death, then has his sentence commuted to life, and in a few short years is back on the streets.
In my riding, like some other large urban ridings, there have been murders. I held in my arms a man who lost his wife and an 18-month old son to a murderer. Not only the family and friends of the murdered victim are lost, but many witnesses who gave testimony at the trial live in fear of their lives as well. They fear for their safety because they know that the accused will possibly be out on a weekend pass or on parole in a few years. The date of parole really becomes a focal point in their lives.
I have a neighbour who lives just around the corner from me who regularly writes to me, and I, in turn, write to the Solicitor General, about a murderer who took his daughter's life. This man also murdered three other women and received ten years imprisonment for each murder, the sentences to run concurrently. What can I answer to this constituent? He knows that the man who murdered the four women is going to be out-I believe 1978 is the last date I was told. How do you answer these people? How do you console them? How can they pick up their lives and start anew? What possible help can we give them? How can we allay their fears when they express their concern about a murderer who is about to be released on parole? "Has he fulfilled his debt to society," they ask? "How do you know he will not do it again?"
It has been suggested that some of the money used to keep prisoners in jail should be used to rehabilitate the family. I think this suggestion is worthy of consideration. Some who have spoken for the abolition of capital punishment have said that if you ever saw a man hang, you would not vote to retain capital punishment. To them I can only say, "If you ever saw a person murdered, you would never vote for abolition; or if you had ever looked into the hopeless faces and hopeless lives of the family of the victim, you would never vote for abolition."

I do not suppose that anything I am going to say here today is going to convince anyone one way or the other, but I should like to say a few words on terrorism. We used to think it could never happen here, that those terrible crimes happened elsewhere, that terrorism could not happen in this country. But in the last few years we have seen that terrorism knows no boundaries, respects no nationality or person. Terrorists kill indiscriminately for money or a cause they believe in. If some innocent victim happens to be passing by, this is his tough luck.
I do not know whether any member of this House has been involved in an incident of terrorism. A few years ago I was travelling on business from Madrid, Spain, to London, England. It was a regular British European Airways' flight. We boarded the plane, and it was held up for a few minutes. At the last moment, several high dignitaries from Spanish Morocco were ushered in and seated in the first-class section. The aircraft taxied out for take-off, and we stopped short of the main runway. Then we were herded off the aircraft and taken some distance away. After a wait of about an hour, the luggage was removed and we were required to look through a heavy steel plate to identify our luggage. There were three pieces of luggage unclaimed, which were removed.
Later, we learned that these three pieces of luggage contained explosives. Someone had called airport officials and warned them that there might possibly be a bomb attack. Along with 75 other innocent people, I might have been the victim of those bombs. Some political or religious group was out to murder the high officials from Spanish Morocco. It was an urgent business trip, and throwing caution to the wind I reboarded the plane and proceeded to London, England. Once we were in the air, those of us who went on wondered whether all the explosives had been removed from the aircraft. Fortunately, they were; but it really was a frightening experience.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot support this bill. I think I have read more on this subject than any other member since coming to parliament. My mail reflects the concern of the people in my riding. I do not want to deal with the statistics of murder. I agree with the Prime Minister that the statistics are generally inconclusive. I have a healthy suspicion of statistics most times, anyway; they can be twisted and turned to support whatever position you wish. But I think one point is missed by those who like to quote them, and that is that the definition of capital murder has been changed several times in the past few years. It differs from country to country and from state to state. The very basis for the statistics, I believe, is faulty to begin with. I am not convinced that a person who commits a premeditated murder can ever be rehabilitated. I am not convinced that he or she can ever become part of society again, as we know it.
As we know, surveys have been taken in the country, and I think that generally speaking they support the position that we should retain capital punishment in Canada. A referendum was taken in California about five years ago which was signed by seven million people; the outcome was a request to restore capital punishment. I believe most of the people in Canada are saying to us that we should retain capital punishment. In a package of documents that we received from the Solicitor General, which accom-
June 15, 1976

panied the bill, he stated in one place that capital punishment was not a deterrent. Yet, Mr. Speaker, when he was interviewed on CTV he stated that he did not feel capital punishment was any greater deterrent than a 25-year sentence. He confused the issue, as he has done so many times. I am not criticizing him for this, Mr. Speaker, but I think he is a bit mixed up. First, he says it is not a deterrent; then he says it is no greater deterrent than a 25-year sentence.
I think it is evident that most Canadians want capital punishment restored because they are recoiling from what they regard as the loose administration of justice which they have had from this government. They have had enough of kidnappers being released after a few years of confinement. They have had enough of police officers being shot down and their murderers escaping the penalty they deserve. They have had enough of giving priority to the criminal, and neglecting the victim. They have had enough of easy parole and leaves, when they find that many parolees become criminals again and leaves of absence become a door of escape. They have had enough of easy bail, when they find freedom given to thugs, hoodlums and addicts who use it to pillage, assault, molest, and murder. They have had enough of all this and are saying to parliament, "Change this and give us some protection under the laws, the kind of protection that Canadian citizens want and used to be confident of receiving."
No one who speaks for the retention of capital punishment has ever suggested that it will prevent all murders. Surely we would not expect that, any more than we would expect that not having capital punishment would prevent all murders. There has never yet been a penalty devised that would restrain everyone. To dismiss the death penalty because it does not eliminate murder should, logically, mean we should abolish prison sentences because they do not eliminate bank robberies. The point is that the threat of capital punishment does deter some people from murder, just as the threat of imprisonment deters some from robbery.
To say that when you have capital punishment you also have some murders is really offering no more evidence than to say that when you have long jail sentences you also have some robberies. We know that. Although the imposition of the prison sentence does not deter some from robbing, pillaging and assaulting, we have reason to believe that the imposition of the supreme sentence, the death penalty, deters some from the act of murder. That is partly why the average man supports the restoration of the death penalty. One can quote all manner of statistics and draw all sorts of graphs to back one's argument, but still find that the common sense, average Canadian thinks the death penalty deters. He knows it deters him and knows it deters others.
I know others want to participate in this debate and I shall not prolong my remarks. I have, as have all my colleagues, received a great deal of correspondence on this subject from constituents. I have heard from high school students, clergymen, learned judges, and lawyers. The correspondence runs 90 to 10 in favour of the retention of capital punishment. I was particularly touched when I received a series of essays on the subject of capital punish-
Capital Punishment
ment, written as an assignment by a group of students in Dundas, Ontario. I was amazed to see, after the positions pro and con had been plotted on a graph, that 86.3 per cent of those high school students between 15 and 18 years of age favoured the retention of capital punishment.
I have discussed this subject with my constituents at meetings in my office, in my constituency and in my home. Overwhelmingly, they urged me to support the retention of capital punishment. I made it known, since I was first elected, that I was in favour of retaining capital punishment. I have said I will keep an open mind, and if someone can convince me that I should take the contrary position, I will consider such arguments. Since the debate of 1973, the capital punishment file in my office has grown larger than all other files. I have read every bit of information I can lay my hands on dealing with both sides of the question. Having read this material, I am not convinced that we should abolish capital punishment. Therefore, when the vote is called I intend to vote against passage of this bill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, capital punishment is a difficult subject with which members of parliament must deal because of the high emotions it generates and the wide and deep variations of opinions among constituents. All wisdom does not reside on one side or other of the question. Those in favour of abolition are sincere, honest and entitled to their opinions. Those who feel that the state should not surrender its right to impose the ultimate sanction in cases of capital murder are also honest and entitled to their opinions. Outside these groups there is an army of sociologists, penal and rehabilitation experts, prison guards, psychiatrists, police officers, all of whom have a right to be heard. There are those who have gone outside the law and who have opinions on this question. There are also the victims and their families and relatives: the still, quiet voices of the victimized, too often not heard in the land.
Those who are opposed to capital punishment may be divided into the following categories: those who oppose on religious or moral grounds, it is wrong to take a life; those who oppose largely on the pragmatic ground that capital punishment is not a deterrent-this includes some newspaper editors-and those who oppose on the ground of miscarriage of justice, which includes many criminal lawyers.
The proponents of capital punishment include, first, those who, on religious or moral grounds, believe in adequate retribution-an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. On that ground, no dentist would be safe. Second, those who believe capital punishment is a deterrent. Third, those who on economic grounds feel it is too expensive to build special prisons to constrain a growing army of killers. Fourth, those who feel that capital punishment remains society's ultimate line of defence against lawlessness, that it is a matter of protection of the individual and that it should not be surrendered. In this group are police officers and a growing number of citizens disturbed about increasing crimes of violence and murder.
Capital punishment is reserved for the capital crime of murder. In our society it has now become applicable only to those who kill police officers and prison guards and, in practical terms, not even to them. Quite a few police officers and guards have been killed and their killers have not been subjected to the ultimate sanction.

June 15, 1976
Capital Punishment
There are many kinds of murder, and perhaps it is useful to look at some of them. Murder, essentially, is the deliberate and cold-blooded taking of a human life. Some people believe that abortion comes within this definition. Curiously enough, some who shudder at taking the life of a person who has deliberately killed another are in favour of removing life from an urborn child. This indicates the contradictions inherent in questions of morality and ethics. The taking of life is not the issue here, because lives are taken every day in hospitals and rarely are there complaints. Doctors stick knives in people, remove their vital organs and place substitute parts in their bodies. This is accepted because the intent is to preserve life, although it is not always successful.
The intent of murder is to deprive a person of the right to live. A question arising out of this is whether one who deliberately takes the life of another person can continue to assert his own right to live. There has been a great deal of talk about crimes of passion, crimes committed in the heat of a moment's aberration, crimes committed to defend or to punish another person. These are regarded as one-shot crimes. The assumption is that a person who has once lost his or her head will not do so again. It is hard to see why this should be the case. The reverse would seem equally logical, and in fact is borne out too often by experience.
When one has gone through all the crimes of passion, crimes committed in the heat of the moment, crimes under emotional stress, and so on, there remains a solid body of criminal activity, including murder, undertaken coldly and deliberately for personal gain or personal advantage. There are people who murder for profit. An example was George Joseph Smith, in England, who drowned half a dozen women in the bath for their insurance. In this category are poisoners, of whom the records of criminality are eloquent. They are seldom caught with the first victim. Sometimes they are never caught.
There are many cases on record of people killing for mean or petty objectives, insurance benefits and similar questions of personal gain. This applies over the entire field of criminality, not merely murder. Arson, robbery, embezzlement, fraud and kidnapping are crimes in which the objective is the personal advantage of the criminal. Such criminals sometimes resort to violence, including murder. Many of those who claim that capital punishment is not a deterrent to murder nevertheless would not want to do away with jail terms for breaking and entering, robbery with violence and similar crimes. They feel that while capital punishment is not a deterrent, a prison term is.
There is a new kind of crime. In recent years we have seen the emergence of a new type of crime-syndicated crime. This has led to a new type of capital crime, syndicated murder or, as it was once described, "murder incorporated." In this category murder is undertaken for a variety of reasons, largely mercenary, or to remove someone in the way of organized crime. Most people take a broad view of this kind of thing and believe that its proper place is on the TV screen or between book covers. Nevertheless, it happens.

With the spread of crime syndicate activities in the field of labour and industry, syndicated murder has made its appearance in those areas. We have also seen the emergence of a particularly evil type of crime once thought to belong to the dark ages, political assassination-not the kind with which we are familiar in this chamber, but with guns and bullets. One need only mention Martin Luther King, the Kennedys, to recall the vileness of this particular type of development. In Canada we had a case in October, 1970.
There has also been a resurgence of the crime of kidnapping, once punishable by death. Some kidnappings, like the Hearst kidnapping, are politically motivated, some motivated by gain, some both. Political motivation is also behind underground guerrilla activities and aircraft hijackings on an international scale. These activities have caused the loss of innocent lives. This kind of international guerrilla violence appears to be beyond control except through the administration of capital punishment. At least, the effect would be to discourage recruiting for movements of international violence.
Whether capital punishment or the threat of capital punishment is a deterrent, or not, I leave to others to resolve. In the context of protecting the rights of individual citizens, this becomes irrelevant. Nor do I intend to embark on statistics to show the rise in crimes of violence of a peculiarly sadistic character, including molestation of the young and helpless. All of these things may be symbols of a sickness in our society. Perhaps Judy LaMarsh can get to the bottom of that phenomenon. What I think can be taken for granted is that there has been, in the past decade, a notable increase in crimes of violence of the kind described above and this may account for the uneasiness of Canadians and their reluctance to surrender the ultimate protection which society affords.
There seems to be an idea abroad that our kind of society, a free society, has no right to defend itself. This is a fatal misapprehension. For many people, the issue is further complicated by a statement from Roman Catholic bishops urging that the state-that is, society-surrender its right to apply the ultimate penalty. The bishops, like others, are within their rights.
This is not, however, a question of faith or morals, and therefore others are equally within their right in disagreeing with the proposal. I know that in the constituency which I represent there is a great deal of uneasiness, in view of the rise in crimes of violence, about any proposal which appears to lessen society's ability to afford protection to its citizens. To many Canadians aware of the various facets of this proposal, the issue resolves itself into a few major considerations: first, the knowledge that there are in society certain classes of criminals who murder coldly and deliberately for personal gain or in line with the objectives of criminal groups or organizations.
In summary, then, many Canadians feel, and will continue to feel, regardless of what this House decides, that they have a right to resort to ultimate action to defend their lives, homes and families. The final consideration arises when an individual is found guilty, after due process of law, of having deliberately and wilfully taken the life of another person or persons. The state has a responsibility to see that society is protected from such a person. The
June 15, 1976

application of a fixed 25-year sentence does not provide the security that citizens feel they must have. Such a sentence will certainly be subjected to immense pressure toward a reduction, and governments which play politics with capital punishment cannot be relied upon not to bow to pressure to reduce the 25-year sentence. Can a 25-year sentence deter, if hanging does not?
The question of the moral responsibility of the state is one which concerns a number of people. There have been suggestions that the state has no right to take life. Let us look at self-defence. Any person has the right to defend his life. Individuals surrender this right to the state, as they surrender the right to make war and collect taxes for public purposes. This does not mean that an indivudal no longer has the right to defend himself. The individual in our society looks to the state to protect him in his daily activities to keep the streets, playgrounds and schoolyards safe. When the state is no longer able to guarantee protection of the individual and his rights, then the individual will resort to other methods.
Most people will feel that inability by the state to guarantee protection of property and person represents a betrayal of the fundamental rights of individuals in a free society. Such rights as protection of property and the person, and defence against aggression, are fundamental in any society, and the state which cannot fulfil these basic duties is inviting a collapse of public confidence.
The assertion of the state's right to exact the ultimate penalty necessary for the protection of the individual in society is not a question of hanging every person found guilty of murder; nor should the issue be placed on that basis. There is no question of that, nor has there been for at least a decade. Is the ultimate sanction necessary? The question is whether society, faced with an increase in crimes of violence and the emergence of new kinds of organized criminal activities, can preserve and guarantee the rights of its members without retaining the ultimate sanction. This does not involve, in any way, the automatic application of capital punishment in all cases. This determination should be taken out of the hands of cabinets and returned to juries, where it belongs.
The effect of placing the question of clemency in the hands of the government has made clemency a political issue of the most blatant kind. Clemency should not be a political football. Clemency should be a matter for juries to recommend on the basis of common sense and a knowledge of the facts. Faced with this issue, cabinets invariably take the road of least resistance, which in political terms means that the law is simply left in abeyance as it has been for several years. This has been a factor undermining the confidence of Canadians in the application of justice. The ultimate sanction should be applied only when there is no recommendation for clemency by a jury. On that basis, very few people in this country will face the penalty of hanging. Society should not be left without the protection which most Canadians feel they are entitled to as a way of safeguarding their lives and the lives of their families.
Finally, the artificial distinction between official protectors of the public peace and the general public should be discarded. A householder beaten to death in his own
Capital Punishment
home-and there have been many such cases-or patrons of a public place overtaken by a gang feud are as much entitled to the full protection of the law as are policemen and prison guards. Again, this is a matter which should revert to the collective wisdom of juries, and where there is no recommendation for clemency, the law should run its course. In this way, justice would be satisfied and at the same time the confidence of Canadians in their system of justice would be restored.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would hope that the matter would be discussed from the standpoint of the government's duty to protect society, rather than "hawkish" appeals to jailhouse sentimentality. There is very little emotionally appealing about someone who deliberately sets out to take away the life of an innocent person for reasons of personal gain, malice or self-aggrandisement. In summary, the question is this: Are we justified in depriving the citizen of his right to protection by the state?
There have been cases in recent months of persons committing murder while already having been convicted of a previous murder. We have granted bail to persons charged with murder. We have even released killers on weekend passes. The result is that citizens are uneasy and feel they are not being protected in the way in which they are entitled. Certainly, a bill which deprives the state of its power to act in protecting citizens from the ultimate crime of murder is not a good bill.
Most people will feel that the threat of 25 years imprisonment is not a good guarantee of protection in the case of a criminal who may already have killed once and may be fleeing from the scene of a crime while heavily armed and dangerous. If the threat of hanging is not a deterrent, why should the threat of 25 years in jail be a deterrent? If hanging is not a deterrent, nothing is. If hanging is not a deterrent, then it is silly to talk of putting criminals behind bars for armed robbery, rape and other crimes of violence. The ultimate conclusion is that nothing is a deterrent and you may as well let them all roam free, which is very nearly the situation at the present time.
A person who coldly and deliberately commits murder- and there are some in that category-forfeits his claim to life. A person found guilty of deliberate murder, under due process of law, certainly cannot claim the right to life, a right of which he has already deprived his victim and, in some cases, more than one victim. It is my contention that only a jury is in a position, having heard the evidence, to make a reasoned judgment on the question of capital punishment. Where a jury does not see fit to recommend mercy, then the government should not put itself in the position of going beyond the intentions of the jury. Under the circumstances, the law should be carried out.
Society must be protected against hijackers, urban guerrillas, professional killers and criminal syndicates part of whose stock-in-trade is murder. Recently, the editor of the Guiness Book of Records in Britain was callously, ruthlessly and deliberately executed for having dared to advocate capital punishment for terrorist killings. A society which cannot protect its own citizens against professional assassins is a society on the way out. It is issuing an invitation to anarchy. Far too many killers are murdering for a second or third time, encouraged by the loopholes and laxity of our laws and our system of criminal administra-

tion and bail requirements. Perhaps these are reasons surveys show that the majority of Canadians feel that for the sake of the protection they are entitled to have from society, the state should not give up the right to impose the ultimate sanction when it is necessary to do so.
That, Mr. Speaker, ends my contribution to this debate. I believe there are other members who would like to say a few more words.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO BUSINESS ACTIVITIES OF CHAIRMAN OF ANTI-DUMPING TRIBUNAL-MOTION UNDER S O.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Before introducing legislation perhaps he might answer a couple more questions. Well, Mr. Speaker, the paper I presented to the provinces, and which was tabled in this House yesterday, answers some of the points raised by the hon. member. It indicates that our proposition would have the effect of helping in a general way the less fortunate provinces because they would not be shared-cost programs; they would not be tied to a 50 cent dollar offered to each province and therefore the poorer provinces would not be dependent on spending their 50 cents in order to get our 50 cents. What we have proposed at this time is an outright transfer either of tax points or cash or in fact a mixture of both. In this way the less fortunate provinces would receive the transfer without having to spend equivalent amounts themselves. This would be advantageous to them in the sense that in the past they have fallen behind in some of the expenditures because they could not afford to put the 50 cents into the program which drew the 50 cents from the federal government.
Now we are saying, you will have it regardless of what you spend, providing you spend our funds which we will offer you or our tax funds in the areas of health and post-secondary education. This seems an advantageous way of bringing more equity to the poor provinces and, more particularly, of not upsetting their priorities. We are not forcing them to enter into a certain field in order to qualify for federal help. They will get the help whether or not they do anything in the fields of health and education.
