speechtext:
My question is with regard to the cost-shared programs and the departure of the government in terms of the open-endedness of those programs. The Prime

Minister insists this is not a departure from traditional policy. However, it seems to be a very important departure from traditional policy. The Prime Minister says the negotiations are open and that he has offered options to the provincial governments. It is the sort of option of whether they want to be shot, hanged or garroted. He said there is a ceiling or cap being put on.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister level with the House of Commons and indicate whether this is a sharp departure from past government policy and if he intends to put a cap on expenditures of the provincial governments in these cost-shared programs?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext:
It is,
indeed, a sharp departure in one sense. It is acceding to what the provinces have been requesting for a long time, namely, that they should be allowed more flexibility in the spending of federal funds, that they would not be obliged to match dollar for dollar everything we spend in these areas of health and education. It is acceding to their request that they should have greater flexibility in the spending of these funds. Then again, the proposals would do away with the necessity for complicated accounting procedure to enable the federal government to see what the provinces are spending in their hospital insurance scheme, and so on. It is a concession to the provinces in another sense: they have been asking for more tax room and this proposal gives them more tax room.
What the hon. member is suggesting is that we are seeking not to make it open-ended. I must concede that he is right in his conception. We are saying we must be able to plan in the future, to know what our costs are likely to be; that they should not be automatically tied to any level of spending by provinces no matter how improvident or fanciful it might be; it has to be predictable so that we can budget properly. It is for this reason we are suggesting a rate of escalation roughly corresponding to the increase in the gross national product. I said to his leader that formula is debatable-we could hear representations with regard to that-but we are suggesting it should not be completely open-ended as was the case, perhaps, in the past.
We have brought before the House measures to cap some of these programs as the bill in the name of the Minister of Finance, presently before parliament, is doing. It is a question of whether we should set growth arbitrarily at a rate of 15 per cent, for instance, or whether we should say the growth ought to be held at a rate equivalent to the growth of the gross national product. A choice can be made. The hon. member who asked this question is a very responsible member and critic on financial matters and he will certainly understand that it is reasonable for the federal government and, indeed, for the provincial governments, to be able to plan future expenditures with some certainty.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I appreciate the right hon. gentleman's estimation of myself as reasonable and I will therefore ask him a reasonable question. I agree with him that governments have to be able to plan and that they should know
June 15, 1976

what their expenditures are likely to be. But that is not the point of the argument. What we are asking is this: why should something as important as health services or education be geared to the percentage growth of the gross national product any more than he would restrict, say, the growth of ESSO to the expansion in the GNP? I ask him whether he is prepared to find a formula which, while it might cap expenditures, would allow the growth of these important public services to be in excess of the increase in the GNP or of historic standards.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I am certainly prepared to consider that proposition if it is put forward by the provinces. To my recollection, and I see the Minister of Finance is agreeing with me-at least, I think he is-the provinces have not made such a proposal. They, too, want to plan their future growth. Hon. members ask: why tie it to the gross national product? The premiers asked, as did hon. members opposite: why tie it to the gross national product? We said: why not? It is a reasonable basis and I explained the basis of that answer to the leader of the New Democratic Party. These are established programs. Health delivery services in Canada are among the best in the world-certainly they are among the most generous, and the arrangements for post-secondary education are very generously financed. It may perhaps be reasonable to say that they should not continue to grow at a rate of 15 per cent or 18 per cent when the economy is growing at a rate of 5 per cent or 10 per cent. That is the proposal we have put forward and which the provinces will consider.
Let me say, also, that this applies to the cash part of the grants. As far as the tax transfer is concerned it is, of course, not tied to anything but the rate of growth of the economy of the province which has the tax point.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT PUTTING CEILING ON SHARED-COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Order!

speechtext: We estimate that the rate of growth will be slightly in excess of that.

subtopic: BASIS OF MINISTER'S VIEWS ON PROVISION OF ELECTRICITY FOR ATLANTIC PROVINCES-POSSIBILITY OF STUDY OF PROBLEM

speechtext:
Yesterday, the hon. member for Palliser, supported by the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, raised a point of order concerning dress in the chamber. Investigation reveals that while there may not be technical rules that are easily interpreted in precise terms, the standard which has been adhered to is that which has been enforced in the discretion of the Chair. Reference was made to the presence in the chamber yesterday of an hon. member who was not wearing a necktie in the ordinary sense of the word as we know it.
Representations have been received from other members, by correspondence, and it would seem appropriate-and I will take the first opportunity that ought to present itself the day after tommorrow-to discuss this matter with the House leaders in order to determine whether some expression of definition on this matter might be forthcoming from members, perhaps from the Committee on Procedure and Organization or the Committee on Management and Members' Services. In the meantime, I would propose that until such expression comes forward from either of the committees, or as otherwise suggested by the House leaders on Thursday, I will continue to rigidly enforce, and expect co-operation from all hon. members, the rules in respect of dress and decorum which have prevailed in this House since, so far as I am aware, its inception, one of which is that male hon. members of this House shall wear a shirt, a tie and a jacket, as has ordinarily been accepted up to this time.
I would indicate that if there is a feeling to the contrary, I would expect all hon. members in the interim to abide by and respect this rule, at least until such time as suggestions are made to the contrary and those suggestions are taken up by the House as a whole.

That this House views with great alarm the ill-considered and illogical decisions of the government which fail to give adequate priority to health research funding.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the third time in the past twelve months I have risen in this House to make a major address on the subject of medical research in this country, and this is because I think it is one of the most important subjects this House could deal with in terms of the effect it has on the ills and the life of Canadians everywhere. I do not think anyone would argue with the fact that medical research is an integral part of the health education system and, indeed, that it is as important as any other aspect of the health care delivery system.
I should like to look at some of the complaints we have heard from around the country resulting from the ill-considered policy the government has been following in regard to medical research and, indeed, in regard to research in general. We heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) before the committee not too long ago indicate that he supports slow growth and expansion of research in general and medical research in particular. If we examine the record of performance, we see there has been a slow but steady erosion of the research dollar on a pretty well continual basis since 1971. Indeed, this year there has been a freeze which has resulted in a substantial cut in research funds and research projects that have been under way for a long time the cut being necessary because of the uncontrolled inflation which still rages in this country.
We have a situation in which the priorities of this government fall under serious question and must be reassessed very carefully. The minister has told us that some 60 researchers left the country in the past year, while 100 have come in from the U.S. I think that if we look at the loss to our country in relation to the size of our population, and the loss to the United States in relation to the size of its population, we can see very clearly that our loss is much greater in terms of time and the cost of training of the people who have been leaving.
Medical Research
We note from the history of two months ago that some 40 per cent of ongoing research projects in this country have been terminated and that of the new applications which number in the vicinity of 400, only 10 per cent were accepted for funding as of April this year. I have here a letter which I want to read, because I think it indicates fairly clearly a story which has been repeated over and over in this country in recent months. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not here. I realize that he has been involved with the federal-provincial conference, but I understand it is now over and it cannot be used as an excuse for his not being here. I am also very sorry that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) is not here, because he is the individual who has a good deal to say about the kind of funding which takes place.
I think the absence of these two ministers indicates very clearly the attitude of the government toward research in general and medical research in particular. This is a shameful situation. Those ministers, who should be here and are not, should be thoroughly scolded by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I will now refer to this letter which comes from a researcher in Ontario, a man involved in the area of eye research. It reads as follows:
At the First International Congress of Eye Research in 1974, of several hundred delegates attending from around the world, I was the only Canadian present. As far as I know, our group is the only one in Canada at present, funded by the Medical Research Council of Canada, which is performing biochemical research on lens differentiation and cataract.
I am sure everyone knows what a cataract is. It is a disorder of the lens of the eye. It "turns the pupil grey" and makes it impossible for the possessor of such an eye to see very clearly. Later, when it becomes worse, the person cannot see at all. The letter continues:
Beginning in 1967, in my laboratory at the University of Western Ontario, we have carefully nurtured a program in research on the development of the eye lens. Studying the regular growth and differentiation of such normal cells may enable us to compare these normal processes to the abnormal ones in cancer cells. With this knowledge we may be better able to define what makes a tumour cell different.
We hope that our program will eventually result in information about the lens protein changes which appear to be the root cause of cataract formation. Such information would be invaluable in preventing certain types of cataract, especially senile cataract.
That refers to a cataract in an old person.
We have developed special techniques for growing cells of the lens outside the body on microscope slides, and in sterile bottles. Using these techniques we hope to be able to test different drugs for their effects in preventing the aggregation of the lens proteins which causes the lens to become milky in cataract. This milkiness may arise in much the same way that an egg white changes from clear to milky white when it is cooked. When scientists find drugs which will prevent this "milkiness" from appearing, or cause it to disappear, we may be able to treat many cataracts by eye drops.
At the present time the only possible treatment for cataracts is surgery. Because of this cataracts remain the leading cause of hospital admissions for eye operations in North America. In addition, approximately 15 per cent of all individuals in the United States who are considered legally blind have cataracts as the underlying cause.
I think the statistics indicate that the disease of cataract of the eye, which represents a leading cost in respect of hospital admissions in North America, could be resolved, with a saving of millions of dollars in respect of surgical

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
and other associated expenses. It is a clear indication that this is the kind of investment which indeed would be an investment rather than an expenditure. The letter continues:
Cataract surgery often is possible only after a long period of waiting for the cataract to ripen. While the cataract ripens, the afflicted person, who is often elderly, must endure a state of near-blindness and restricted activity. Both of these are bad for his attitude and over-all health.
Until this year, the main support for this research has been obtained from the Medical Research Council of Canada, and we have painstakingly built up a small team of research workers in my laboratory whose salaries and whose experiments are funded by an annual grant from the Medical Research Council.
The latest government funding increase to the Medical Research Council has limited its total budget to $48 million instead of the $55 million requested. My grant has been terminated. This means that I am to be granted only enough funds to keep my laboratory running until the end of November. Before then the team will be broken up, as some workers in the laboratory seek other employment. So even if the project were to be reinstated then, when the Medical Research Council meets again, much valuable time would be lost. If no last minute reprieve comes, Canada will have lost perhaps its only biochemical research group on lens development and cataract.
This gentleman touches pretty well on the key points with which we are concerned. I am sorry to see that the former minister who was recently evicted from the cabinet is scoffing at this whole business and seems to think it is funny that medical research is being cut, with the result that hundreds of projects are being disbanded and research teams are being disbanded and asked to undertake other work. If he thinks this is funny, I hope he will have the courage to get up in this House and explain this to the research people and to the citizens of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I do not know the name of the riding of the hon. member who just interjected, but perhaps that is a good thing. He is from Toronto, in any event, and he seems to exemplify the attitude other members on that side have taken. When a group known as Canadians for Health Research came to Ottawa on May 20 of this year and were receivd by members of the government party, rather than listen to the proposals and the brief presented by the group known as Canadians for Health Research, the Liberals at that time decided to assault the group for blackmailing the government because they expressed their views publicly.
Instead of taking a serious look at the problem, the Liberals took the position that the researchers were simply blackmailing the government for some kind of political motive. I think nothing could be further from the truth. The President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have indicated that the freeze on medical research is necessary because we are in a period of restraint, and that somehow this kind of freeze will save Canadians millions of dollars. Because of that statement I want to point out the kind of savings successful research has produced for Canada and for the world.
First, I want to look at the field which is known as immunology. I have here a report from the United States which indicates that expenditures in research are very minor in nature in comparison with the savings which a country achieves in terms of hospital and medical costs. I am referring to a brief which was sent to our committee by

a researcher from the University of Manitoba. I should like to quote from it.
The brief suggests that the eradication of polio, which was dependent on basic Canadian research leading to the development of the Salk vaccine, is saving the U.S. treasury $2 billion a year. The discovery of the measles vaccine is saving about $180 million a year. Basic research alone on the eradication of Rh hemalytic disease in the newborn, by Dr. Bruce Chown of the University of Manitoba, is saving $60 million a year. The identification of the transfusion hepatitis virus is saving $100 million a year. Organ transplant immunology and replacement of dialysis is saving another $100 million a year.
Considering this very restricted area of research, namely, immunology, the conclusion was that based on the annual immunology research budget of $33 million, the annual cost benefit was $3.3 billion. In other words, the saving in hospital and other costs required to treat these diseases which were formerly not preventable was about 100 to 1, or for every $1 invested in research in immunology there has been a saving of $100 in the long run. I think that quite clearly shows that if the minister feels he is saving money for Canadians by cutting the health research budget, he is indeed misinformed and doing Canada a great disservice.
We have also heard members of the cabinet suggest that we do not really have to do research in this country because we can simply read the health journals and get without cost the finds of research done in other countries. I think that is a most irresponsible position to take. As a matter of fact, the minister who proudly lays claim to that view, the minister of science and technology, is in the House, and I am glad to see him here because I want him to know that this party disapproves vigorously of such an approach. Indeed, as a Canadian I am ashamed that a minister of our government would talk like that. That attitude can only bring us losses.
One of the factors we must consider is that if we have no well developed researchers, no well developed and well trained scientists in a given field, essentially what we have is no one accurately to interpret the research which is being done in other countries. Secondly, we know from past experience that if we have a well developed research centre located in our country at one of the universities, that centre attracts some of the best research people in the field, the result is that we have the best research people available in the world to teach our physicians, and thus we wind up with the best educated physicians possible.
So I do not think that we can accept the statement of the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) that we do not have to spend money on research ourselves, that we can simply act as parasites and take it from other countries and be as well off in the long run. That is another fallacy which I want to dispel.
If you look at our expenditures on health research in comparison with that of other countries-and I think the best country with which to compare ourselves is the United States-you will find that we are behind them. They are spending in the vicinity of four or five times the amount that we are spending, on a per capita basis. The result is that researchers who are not being funded adequately here often go south of the border where funds
June 15, 1976

seem to be much more easily available. What we have in this country is a government which claims to be committed to medical research but its actions have proven otherwise. We have had a "stop and go" policy in funding, making it virtually impossible to develop a feeling of stability and security in the research community.
I want to make some suggestions in the course of my remarks, in the hope that someone will take note of them. What we need is long-term planning incorporating a policy of long-term stability in the research field. There are several reasons for that, one of them being that it takes some 12 years to train a medical researcher at considerable cost, and it takes a number of years to assemble a research team, laboratory technicians and other workers, and to get a project under way. It seems almost criminal to decide, for no particular reason, to dismember such a team and to create a situation where the head of the team must either leave the country if he wants to continue research, or go into some other field of work. None of these reasons make good, logical sense.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare announced recently that there was to be a $2 million addition to the Medical Research Council funding for this year. That happens to be about 30 per cent of the amount required to bring research in this country up to last year's level. I suggest that what must be done immediately is a further $4.6 million allocation in order to allow the researchers to continue at last year's level. We, as a party, want to put forward a long-term policy, and I think a good suggestion that we should aim for is to not only stay at last year's level of activity in Canada but over the next five years catch up with the United States, West Germany, Sweden and other countries which so far have been ahead of us in terms of funding of medical research. This is an objective which this party has accepted as party policy.
The other things which we must consider are to accept once and for all that medical research is part and parcel of the health care delivery system and must be given adequate attention at all times to ensure that it survives and flourishes in this country. We must also consider giving sufficient funding and sufficient commitment to research to ensure that there is an adequate research base for education in the health field, to make sure that there is an expansion of scientific and technical knowledge as a basis for health care. We must improve the application of scientific principles to health care; we must support adequate training of research investigators in the health field and, finally, we must support research contributions to new knowledge in the health field.
Even though it may have been somewhat clumsily expressed, I have just outlined what I think would be an excellent long-term policy with the long-term objective of bringing Canada up to par with other developed countries in the world in the area of medical research. We recognize that we cannot be best in all fields. We agree, perhaps, that we should be doing more research in the areas in which we are particularly capable. At the same time, we must ensure that we have adequately trained people in a wide variety of fields. Perhaps we can work in some aspect of every field, although not in all aspects of every field. Only in this way can we expect that in the long term Canadians will be the beneficiaries of the best health care system in the
Medical Research
world. In the long run this is also the only way we can expect to improve the health care delivery system as far as keeping costs down and providing proper education for individuals who are providing our medical services.
The item I read at the beginning of my comments which dealt with an eye research project was of particular significance because the funding the researcher asked for was in the vicinity of $22,000 for this year to keep his project going. I want to point out very dramatically the kind of priorities this government decides upon when it cuts research into the development of cataracts on the eye. The Ottawa Citizen of March 23 ran a picture of an office, with the caption in big, black letters:

Urban affairs minister Barney Danson's office in the restored La Salle Academy on Sussex Drive, was enhanced by $37,400 worth of restoration work to return it to its original 19th century splendour.
I wonder whether there is something wrong with the priorities of the government, when it spends $37,400 on an office to bring it to its nineteenth century splendour but does not have $22,000 to fund a project on cataract
research.
Hear, hear!
I think the fact that it was nineteenth century splendour reflects the thinking of this government which is perhaps even earlier than that century.
Seventeenth century.

The middle ages, or dark ages. I think that is where we are going if this government remains for very much longer.
I am glad to see the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) in the chamber. He is also guilty of the misuse of funds. A satellite was launched last fall, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you received a great, glossy brochure with pictures and beautiful drawings, the total cost of which was $17,000. I should like the minister to stand in this House and tell us why that brochure was necessary. What did it do to help the satellite perform its function? Was it really necessary? Could he not simply have written a letter and had his secretary type it to explain that a satellite was going up in the sky? That would not have cost anything. But to pay for the brochure, a research project somewhere in this country had to be cancelled. I have an example of such a project right here, Mr. Speaker.
Here is a letter from a researcher at the University of Manitoba who was trying to develop a method of treating cancer using the concept of immunology. This project was initiated in 1972-73 as a result of a pioneering observation that if particular drug-induced tumours of guinea pigs are infiltrated with certain kinds of cells they are able to kill rapidly-growing tumour cells in a test-tube. After an encouraging initial funding by the Medical Research Council for the next two years, an increase barely equivalent to the inflation rate was given, which was followed by a serious cut and a terminal grant this year. The project is

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
now being terminated-and all that was needed for this year was $18,000.
If the Secretary of State had not spent $17,000 on that fancy brochure, this cancer research project could have survived and may have found a cure for cancer. I hope the Secretary of State who is sitting there scratching his beard, feels very guilty about that gross abuse and misuse of public funds. There is a gross mix-up in what the priorities of this country should be. It seems to me that the only solution to overcome all the serious problems is to replace a government that has so little concern for the health of Canadians.
Hear, hear!

I should like the ministers to whom I have referred to look around this chamber and tell me which of their colleagues they would not mind dropping from a heart attack in the next year, or which one of their colleagues. I see the Minister of State for Science and Technology pointing at me, Mr. Speaker. That is very unkind of him, and I am sure he does not mean it. I should like him to look around on his own side and see which of his colleagues he would not mind dropping of cancer in the next five years or so.
That is exactly what is happening, with research. Instead of facing the problem and realizing the importance of it and funding it, we have an expenditure of $1.5 billion on Petro-Canada, a totally unnecessary structure. I do not know how many hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent on the Canada Development Corporation for no reason except political expediency. There is no way anybody can point to a need in this country for the Canada Development Corporation, yet it is using up hundreds of millions of dollars. Nobody can say that medical research is not useful or is not needed, yet it is being totally ignored. I cannot understand that. I have some other suggestions to make, Mr. Speaker. The average amount of money requested for many of the research projects which have been cancelled-

Order, please. I regret that I have to interrupt the hon. member, but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my gratitude to hon. members. I thought they on the other side were asleep, and perhaps that is the only reason they allowed me to carry on. But because of their curtesy I shall try to wind up very quickly.
The Prime Minister's swimming pool could have funded ten research projects-$250,000 divided by 25, and you have ten research projects. Then there is the Canada Development Corporation, which you can figure out for yourself. If we abandoned Petro-Canada and put that money into medical research, there would be no need to seek money elsewhere, not only to match medical research in the United States but to surpass it. It seems to me that if the members of cabinet, who control spending in this country, gave the matter some thought, they could only come to the

conclusion that their priorities must be re-examined, changed and placed in the proper order so that Canadians could receive what they expect from their government. They should have the kind of funding for medical research to which people residing in a well developed, industrialized, western nation are entitled. Until this is done, I am afraid there is no way that I can support this government in anything it does.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House in the name of the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), criticizing, as it does, the failure of the government to give adequate priority to health research funding, is timely. Not only is it timely in a general sense; it is significant in that it is being debated this very day when the federal government has taken a stand with the provinces in which it has produced a total package of which changes with respect to health research funding is a significant part. We want to indicate our full support of the criticism implied in this motion. If I may say so without calling for too many retorts from my friends of the Progressive Conservative party, I think we support this motion more strongly than they do.
I do not understand.

I was hoping an hon. member would interject so that I could explain what I have in mind. The motion being debated in the House today has been moved by a Progressive Conservative member and it has the support of that party. At the same time, Progressive Conservative premiers, such as Premier Lougheed and Premier Davis, are saying they are satisfied with the fiscal rearrangements the federal government is proposing.
That is a non sequitur.

The two positions are completely and totally unrelated. When any provinces, especially wealthy provinces, agree to a rearrangement of the fiscal priorities of this country so that less wealthy provinces have to work that much harder for health and education, it means that the federal government will feel it can cut back on medical research funding or, at least, not keep such funding in line with the cost requirements of that research. I hope that my hon. friends to my right who have taken an important and significant stand in the House on this matter today, as they have on other occasions, will have some heart-to-heart talks with the conservative premiers of the wealthy provinces.
If Canada is to be one country from coast to coast, a country in which Canadians across this land have an equal opportunity to participate in important and essential services, I suggest that we must make a better deal for our people than the sort of deal which has resulted from the last two days of federal-provincial conference. As I say, that conference dealt generally with post-secondary education and health in all its aspects, but the question of medical research and funding for such research is part of the whole package. If the government, with the blessing of Premier Lougheed and Premier Davis, gets away with providing less money to the provinces for health services,
June 15, 1976

it will also get away with providing less money for medical research. In our view, this situation is most serious. All that has been highlighted by what happened yesterday and today, and it is of great importance to Canada.
I agree with my friends of the official opposition about the particular importance of funding for medical research. Answering questions today, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) seemed to have a great deal to say about a particular cliche, namely, that we should not spend at a rate faster than the growth of the gross national product. Actually, I have seldom seen the Prime Minister as excited as he was today. He walked out into the aisle farther than I have ever seen him walk since he became Prime Minister. On two occasions he turned round and addressed himself to members of the Liberal party. That was his only way of getting applause.
That was one of our finer parliamentary moments.

That cliche sounds plausible. The proposition that one's expenditures should not increase by more than the growth of the gross national product certainly should apply to total expenditures, whether one is speaking of a state or a person. But it is also true that a person or state can rearrange spending priorities. Although our total expenditures may not increase beyond the increase in revenues, or the increase in the gross national product, it is still desirable and possible to cut down on some other things to make sure that we can adequately and properly fund health delivery services and health research. We contend, therefore, that the government's policies are shortsighted and unfair to the Canadian people, both of this generation and of future generations, in that they do not provide for the maintenance of adequate funding for medical research.
I presume we shall be given figures today to show that more dollars will be spent this year than were spent last year, and perhaps more dollars will be spent next year than this year on medical research. But everyone in this House knows that we are concerned not just about the number of dollars but about the value of those dollars. Unless the number of dollars spent in this area increases in proportion to today's costs, it means that a cap has been put on expenditures, or funding for medical research has been frozen. The result will be that persons engaged in medical research will have to give up their projects, go elsewhere, or what have you, and Canadians both of this and future generations will suffer thereby. With all these considerations in mind, we welcome the present opportunity to speak on this subject today. We regret that the rules of the House do not allow us to vote on this motion. If we could vote, we would support the motion.
I know that we all get letters when an issue of any importance comes up. Perhaps reading from letters is not the most hard working way to make a speech. When I looked at my file today, I found many letters on this subject. I confess I was impressed by the number of letters I received from doctors and professors of medicine across the country, particularly from my own city of Winnipeg. The hon. member for Athabasca spoke of some researchers in my city. I do not intend to read at length from letters, but I do wish to indicate the kinds of persons from whom I
Medical Research
have received letters on this subject. Many of them have also written to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), or the Prime Minister. Copies of those letters were sent to me.
I was sent a letter by Dr. J. C. Haworth, professor of paediatrics, director of clinical investigation and research at the Children's Health Sciences Centre in Winnipeg. Another letter came from Professor Alec Sehon, director of the medical research council group for allergy research of the faculty of medicine, University of Manitoba. Another letter came from Professor Frank S. LaBelle, department of pharmacology and therapeutics, faculty of medicine, University of Manitoba, in Winnipeg. Next, one came from Professor Roma Z. Hawirko, department of microbiology, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg. Then there is a letter from Dr. Victor Chernick, of the department of paediatrics, University of Manitoba. Actually, he is paediatrician in chief at the children's centre. Then I got a letter from Sister Ruth C. Hickey, who is vice-president of St. Boniface General Hospital in Winnipeg. There is also a letter from Professor Peter E. Dresel of the department of pharmacology and therapeutics, faculty of medicine, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg.
Professional people of that calibre and standing in the community, busy as they are, do not take time to write letters to the government or members of parliament unless the issue about which they write is of deep concern. As I say, most of the letters I have had are letters which have also been sent to various responsible ministers. All the letters make the same point strongly: this cutback is a case of false economy. By cutting back on funding for health research, or limiting funding in such a way that health research cannot be carried on, we are betraying Canadians of this and future generations. I mentioned a number of letters that I received, all of them from Winnipeg. I would like to mention one letter that came from somewhere else in the country because I want to quote briefly from it. It is from Dr. H. Arnold Steinberg, chairman, Canadians for Health Research, whose address is Westmount, Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I thought I would get a response from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) on that. The Minister of Public Works is also the Minister of State for Science and Technology, and I gather that is the capacity in which he will be dealing with this matter. It is always good to have him on these subjects, although I had hoped the Minister of National Health and Welfare might have been here as well. At any rate, I want to read a couple of paragraphs from Dr. Steinberg's letter because I think it sums up what most of these letters have said. I quote:
The quantity and quality of medical research affects every Canadian in two principal ways: 1. It is the only practical answer to reducing health care costs by finding cures to those diseases which randomly strike thousands of people necessitating government expenditures now in excess of $7 billion annually.
That point in itself should be enough to move this government to reconsider its position. One sure way to decrease the cost of medical care is to do something about

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
medical research. I quote the second point set out in Dr. Steinberg's letter:
2. Most outstanding physicians and surgeons are attracted to those teaching hospitals that carry on active research programs, a majority of which are funded by the Medical Research Council. While allowing a 16 per cent increase in overall expeditures, the government has frozen the MRC budget at last year's level. This has caused a major cutback in medical research activity. Leading investigators are being forced to move elsewhere to conduct their research work. This will have a profound impact on the quality of hospital care and on the quality of teaching of medicine across the country.
We are dealing with something that is extremely serious. As I have already said, the decisions made, or at least handed down, by the federal government at the conference centre over the past day or two have been very serious for the future of this country. I suggest the most serious of all is what is being done in the field of health.
There is one other quotation I should like to read from one of my many letters from doctors. This comes from Dr. Peter E. Dresel of Winnipeg, to whom I have already referred. I quote this because I think it makes the point very clear.
Because the budget of this council-
The reference is to the Medical Research Council.
-is already so small, because it has not kept pace with inflation in the costs of research for some years, and because it supports a very high percentage of all medical research in Canada, the budget freeze will cause inordinate damage to Canadian medicine. Medical research is a prerequisite to good medical teaching and is basic to medical practice and the delivery of health care. The development of young teacher-scientists and of clinicians with skill in investigative medicine must remain a high priority for a government interested in the future welfare of the Canadian people.
Canadian researchers are in general agreement that government spending must be controlled.
That, of course, fits in with the line of thinking of the government. Although a copy of this letter was sent to me, the original was sent to the Minister of Finance.
They do not ask for special treatment, but only that the guidelines of limited increases be applied to extramural research as they are to all government efforts.
In my view, the fact that so many professors and doctors, experts in the health field, are expressing this kind of concern underlines the seriousness of this issue. I hope the government can be persuaded by this day's debate. It is in addition to other days we have had on this subject to review the position with respect to the way it is treating the Medical Research Council and, in turn, medical research in this country.
I have referred to various letters from professionals in the health field, doctors and professors. I have another letter I should like to read. It does not come from the medical field itself, but from one of the societies that is concerned about a particular disease, the ravages of which hit a great many Canadians. I shall read from the spring, 1976, publication of the Multiple Sclerosis Society of Canada. On one page of this report there is an open letter signed by Peter J. Lowry, the president of that society. It is headed "Tell your MP", and reads as follows:
I'm mad. And you should be too. Our federal government is sticking its head so far into the sand on the question of medical research funding that the only part of the legislators' anatomy still above ground is that part which offers the right amount of flesh for a good kick.

Sure, I believe in restraint in government spending. But not when the end result could be the further weakening of our ability to do medical research in this country. The federal government has restricted the growth of Medical Research Council funds to the point that we are in danger of losing many of our best researchers. This is not just shortsighted or stupid; it's a crime against future generations of Canadians.
It has been said that some members of the federal cabinet believe that Canada can just import medical research because it is too expensive for Canada to make a contribution. Obviously that kind of thinking was not around when Canada gave insulin to the world. Wiser Parliaments in the past have given Canada a strong and vital medical research capability and the momentum has to be maintained.
We are working too hard in this Society to raise funds for research to see the ground cut out from under us by federal penny-pinching. The basic funding has to be done by the government. Funds for MS research cannot be spent on the facilities or administration of research centres- our funds are for work on solving the mystery of MS. Even the funds from the Cancer Society and the Heart Foundation are inadequate to fill the gap being left by the federal government.
So, tell your MP. Tell you friends to tell their MP. If you don't and your friends don't, then your MP will continue to think that nobody cares about medical research. Tell your MP that you care. Write him or her a friendly letter saying you care. Don't send an unfriendly letter- they are probably getting too many of those; or just send this editorial-they'll get the message. You don't need to put a stamp on it if you mail it to your MP at the House of Commons, Ottawa.
I have brought two types of quotations before the House. One is the professional opinion of doctors and professors in our medical schools. But I have read Mr. Lowry's letter because it represents the view of one society that is working in a particular disease area, trying to help the people who suffer from it. I suspect that represents the thinking of the lay people who work in all kinds of societies that are concerned with health problems. This is a very serious situation. It is enough to make some people angry, as Mr. Lowry says in his letter. I hope the government will seriously consider the message that this House is trying to give to it today; that it is false economy and a betrayal of Canadians, both now and in the future, not to provide adequate funding for medical research in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the mover, the hon. member for Athabaska (M. Yewchuk), who is giving us an opportunity today to deal with a subject on which I feel very strongly since the last budget was introduced because this government does not give health research financing the importance it should have.
Every time I had an opportunity to do so I constantly drew the attention of the government to those deficiencies, and asked it to review its policy on medical research, particularly at the university level. I am happy to hear today what the first two parties of the opposition that preceeded me had to say so the whole opposition could rise to protest the government's policy on research and be the spokesmen for the entire medical corps, all students, all research technicians across Canada who blame and particularly urge this government to come back on its position in the area of research.
On March 29, 1976, dealing with that famous Anti-Inflation Act I pointed out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) that he was imposing a freeze in priority areas such as assistance to university research while at the same time increasing budgets like national defence or construe-
June 15, 1976

tion of federal buildings. Later on, as reported in issue No. 54 of April 12, 1976, I asked the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) at a sitting of the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, as follows:
Mr. Minister, I was listening to you a while ago, I do not have a copy of your statement, but you mentioned increases, mainly concerning cost-sharing programs with the industry for industrial research. Is it the intention of your government in the future to go for these cost-sharing programs and to progressively abandon the research made by the universities?
Here is what the minister replied:
Mr. Chairman, as I said a while ago, the researches made by the universities are at a high level comparatively to other western countries and Japan.
Always that comparison with other countries without wondering about the needs of this country.
But the need for industrial research is more urgent; this is more evident in the industry and mostly in the private industry, which we are trying to upgrade as much as possible, through all of our assistance programs, which are cost shared programs, as you mentioned a while ago.
We want to keep on doing that, but at the same time, I think we should not neglect anything and permit a small increase for the research in the universities which is also very important for the graduates.
Coming back to this matter, I suggest this is moderate in my view, being a 4 per cent reduction only as compared to other areas. Don't you believe that such restraint may be responsible for the loss of many scientific researchers? The minister answered, and I quote:
I think there will be loss, not as much of our scientists than of the technicians, whose salaries increase every year. That is good as far as the industry is concerned; if they quit the university to go to the industry where they are needed, that is not a bad thing. But if they quit their research to do something else, then, that is a total loss. Unfortunately, this year, there will be a decrease in the number of laboratory technicians in the universities due to the salary increase of the technicians and there will be no comparable increase of money supplied in the budgets of the universities.
This means, Mr. Speaker, the minister was aware of our losses of technicians and university research scientists.
I put another question to the minister:
Looking through the past years, I notice, unfortunately that our research people, you say you would be happy if they went to Canadian industry, but unfortunately they leave the country. Going to the States, I was surprised to meet many Canadians whose studies we have financed and who are down there because they cannot live in Canada.
They cannot find work in Canada and use their knowledge to serve their country. I talked with those people and it is not because they want to live out there, it is because they could not live here.
Do you think that danger will grow by decreasing the reasearch budget of the universities? It is nice to say that the industry needs them, we will try to supply them to the industry, but they have to be trained.
The minister also tells us that he is well aware of that problem but he cannot do otherwise. I think we have got evidence. I want to quote from a letter which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) quoted a few moments ago. I thought he was going to quote the name of the group. Let me complete his quotation by simply naming the group of medical researchers whose letter he quoted:
I wrote to this particular group asking it to describe itself. I received the following answer:
Medical Research
About three months ago, the medical research group was created on the initiative of a group of responsible citizens, of organizations of voluntary people and medical researchers following the government decision to freeze the budget of the Medical Research Council. After only a few meetings, the movement now gathers citizens from one ocean to the other and the groups are made up of thousands of Canadians from all over the country.
I think the minister knows something about this group because not only they came to meet Mr. Steinberg but they also came to meet us and the minister too.
The organization has several major objectives including drawing the attention of the public to the role played by medical research in the daily activities of each Canadian.
This is followed by the passage read by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I shall not repeat this passage, but I would simply like to mention, after I met this group of university physicians who are called active researchers, what we can deduce from the protests made by these research groups:
According to official government estimates for 1976-77, the three subsidized councils will have the same amount as last year for university research:
Mr. Speaker, the same amount with a cost of living increase of 12 to 15 per cent means a reduction.
Canada Council, $27.7 million Medical Research Council, $48.8 million National Research Council, $91.3 million
Last year, the NRC gave out $78.9 million in scholarships and research grants. The present disagreement concerns only the bookkeeping of the government. For instance, for 1976-77, grants in the field of atomic research were included in the NRC budget and the difference between last year's budget and that for 1976-77 is nearly entirely allocated to atomic research.
And the department says: We have not reduced grants! If everything is aimed at atomic research, how can you operate a research project?
The same estimates show that the federal government will increase its expenditures by about 16 per cent. In that case, why should scientists suffer greater restrictions than the government since the freeze it has imposed will mean the elimination of 10 to 15 per cent of all research projects?

subtopic: ACCOUNT OF RECENT MEETING BETWEEN MINISTER C. M. DRURY AND 80 RESEARCHERS FROM OTTAWA UNIVERSITY

speechtext:
Here are a few questions that the researchers asked:
Researchers: They are trying to convince the minister that the combined effect of the lack of government assistance and inflation are endangering research efforts in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ACCOUNT OF RECENT MEETING BETWEEN MINISTER C. M. DRURY AND 80 RESEARCHERS FROM OTTAWA UNIVERSITY
speechtext:
He said repeatedly that we were living in a year of restrictions and that everybody should make the sacrifices necessary to stop inflation.
This is not what is being done at national defence, Mr. Speaker.
Researchers: In their opinion, the current financial conditions discourage young graduates from going into research. They wonder where future scientists will come from.
We probably wait for them to come up from the United States, while we force ours to go over there. And the question is the following:
Question-Does the government intend to support only the best research and let the remaining aside? Does the government realize that

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
the scientists who are forced to leave research will never go back to it? Has it considered the impact of such a loss? Will these people be able to find adequate jobs elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ACCOUNT OF RECENT MEETING BETWEEN MINISTER C. M. DRURY AND 80 RESEARCHERS FROM OTTAWA UNIVERSITY
speechtext:
He disappointed his audience by answering only to the last question, saying that if those highly educated people were unable to get a job elsewhere, it is because the university was doing a bad job ...
That is easy to say, Mr, Speaker. You get all the evidence you want when you visit universities, and meet groups of graduate researchers and you can see how sincere and dedicated they are; when a minister dares speak that way, I find it a bit exaggerated.
There is no doubt that the freeze ordered by the government does not represent a decision based on a scientific policy but rather a financial decision. Indeed, when he was asked in the House whether he was aware that the recent cuts would be a mortal blow to researchers, the Hon. Jean Chretien, president of the Treasury Board, replied that he did not agree with that assumption. The scientists note two long-term effects from those cuts: the manpower problem and that of the level of health care. As for manpower, the scientists are concerned that researchers who will be dismissed will never come back, that many technicians will lose their jobs and that the young scientists will not have an opportunity to make a career in research.
Recently, two University of Manitoba professors wrote to the federal members to explain the importance of manpower. About health care, the Canadian College of Medical Geneticists stated the following:
Solutions to problems and the practical application of knowledge can only be provided by active research programs undertaken in Canada. As professionals involved in genetics, we regret that Canadians at every level will eventually have to suffer from those short-term budgetary decisions.
You have heard the voices of a group of university researchers across Canada. I have in my hand the opinion of the Quebec researchers: "Quebec researchers look at the future with cautious confidence". I do not have time to read the whole document but it is significant that they said, quote:
Quebec researchers are badly affected by the financial crisis involving university research in Canada. Quebec researchers are emerging from this long and hard winter of cuts in financial research more determined than ever while at the horizon there seem to appear the first signs of the unfreezing of federal sources of financing.
The crisis prompted them to tighten their ranks and work together to join the common front of Canadian scientists for a pressure campaign on Ottawa. Then, they mentioned in this article the most critically affected areas, among which, medical biology. As for biology, I had the opportunity, during the year, to follow from a distance a group of researchers in the University of Ottawa. There I was able to realize the plight of those groups, in the field of finance and equipment. The trouble they had getting the material necessary for their projects. Not only did they have difficulty to raise the funds necessary for their projects, 50 per cent only since they gave 50 per cent of their time for nothing-but they did not even have enough money to buy instruments and material for their projects. It is then that I saw the shortcomings or the lack of understanding of the government in the area of university research.
Recently I met the Canadian association of professors in the University of Ottawa who had sent me this letter which I quote:
You are no doubt already aware that the Minister of Health has announced that the freeze on medical research financing is lifted and that the council would get an additional $2 million. Surely this is good news for the researchers who are members of our association. This will allow a number of research teams to keep going, which would otherwise have been, as you have underlined, broken up because of lack of funds. Nevertheless, this increased funding does not make allowance for cost increases brought about by the current inflation rate.
In our opinion, however, it is rather unreasonable that the government should increase subsidies for the Medical Research Council without increasing those for university research done under the National Research Council and under the Canada Council. The National Research Council finances university research in non-medical fields such as agriculture, forestry, biology, chemistry, physics and geology. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all those who have spoken so far have suggested that perhaps the government should take another look at its priorities. Some of their suggestions were thoughtful, but some were, unfortunately, a little less than ludicrous. I will comment on those suggestions later.
In relation to the question of priorities, perhaps one should look at this problem of research, particularly medical research, in the larger perspective. We have in Canada quite an investment in research which is carried out in a number of ways, a number of places and funded from a number of sources. One should recognize that research, basically, is an investment in the future, and to the extent it is not done one is not being prudent in preparing for the future. If all one's wealth and resources are devoted to research, namely, an investment in the future, then the present never arrives. We have to strike a balance between making adequate investment in the future, based on an act of faith, and enjoyment of the present.
A survey conducted in this country in 1973 by OECD indicates that on a per capita basis research in industry in Canada appeared, by comparison with similar research being done in other countries, to be virtually at the bottom of the list. We ranked ninth. When one looks at the quantum of research in Canada in industry, compared with the quantum of research in other OECD countries in industry, he will find we ranked nine out of ten countries. Having regard to research done in government laboratories, on a per capita basis Canada ranked third among OECD countries. Clearly, by this measure we are doing a fair proportion, if all the others are right, of our research in government and a very low proportion indeed in industry.
In respect of research in universities and institutions of higher education, we ranked fourth among OECD countries, exceeded on a per capita basis only by Sweden, Germany and the Unites States. This indicates that our effort must urgently be on the highest priority for fostering research and innovative processes in the manufacturing industry where we are away behind our industrial competitors, the other OECD countries. To this end, a number of government incentive programs were devised. There was a general decision taken that here is where all the additional resources we can find should be directed toward installing more research or more innovative capacity in industry, given that in comparison with our OECD competitors we were up at the top of the procession in respect of research conducted in and by the institutions of higher learning and universities. It is against this background that one looks at the numbers which have been brought out today. I would suggest that far from lagging behind in respect of research, including medical research conducted in the universities in teaching hospitals, Canada ranks high compared to the OECD countries which should provide a reasonable basis for comparison.
I should point out that what we classify in Canada as medical research is performed or is funded or supported not only by the Medical Research Council but by some other agencies. In fact there is, in the current year, devoted to medical research something in the order of $100 million, and in round numbers about half of that comes through the

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
Medical Research Council. Another fraction, about $12 million, comes from the Department of National Health and Welfare quite independently and distinct from the Medical Research Council. The balance, about $35 million, is funded by institutes of higher education, by provincial governments and, very importantly, by private organizations which this year will be putting up some $20 million.
This means that today, when one directs attention purely to the phenomenon or the mechanism of the Medical Research Council, one is not referring to the whole medical research structure. However, the Medical Research Council, as I think everyone will agree, is in the process of doing very good and very useful work. There is little, if any, suggestion that any of the money put through the Medical Research Council is ineffectively or wastefully used. This is my own view, which I believe is shared by most members of the House. But the Medical Research Council is a relatively recent creation.
Some years ago the medical research on behalf of the federal government was largely carried out by the National Research Council. In the 1960s the Medical Research Council was brought into existence as a separate granting council and it has grown from nothing, then, to the position where it has a budget currently, as I indicated, of very close to $50 million per annum. Its growth in terms of funds available to it in the period 1970-71 to 1975-76 has been of the order of 49 per cent in current dollars, or 1 per cent in real terms. Those who talk about cutbacks even in real terms are unaware of the fact that there has been no slipback in respect of real improvement in the Medical Research Council during that period.
If one looks at the period 1970-71 to and including the current year, the rate of growth in nominal terms has been 61 per cent, which is not a bad rate of growth over a period of some seven years. In the same period there has been a real growth in the order of 2 per cent. This, then, is the answer to those who talk of cutbacks.
I am not suggesting for a moment that this is all the Medical Research Council wants, nor indeed all a great many of us here in this House would like to see put at the disposal of the Medical Research Council or, indeed, the other granting councils for research purposes. Prudent people-and I think most members of this House are prudent-like to see the largest possible investment in the future while still meeting current demands which have to be met. In the current year I think we are all sharing in this process of endeavouring to limit the growth in expenditures by all Canadians, including the federal government. This process of limiting growth is a difficult one. It is one in which I think everyone, including researchers and medical researchers, would want to play their part. As I say, even in real terms, discounting inflation, the Medical Research Council over the period 1970 to 1976 has shown a real growth as I indicated.
A number of instances have been put forward where researchers have felt that their particular grants had either been limited or terminated unreasonably. Certainly, the termination or limitation was a source of intense dissatisfaction. However, in real terms the funds have been growing year by year and the allocation of those funds, both those that are continuing and the increases, is made on the basis of value judgment by the doctors' peers. This, I

think-and most people would agree-is the best system we have been able to devise to get the fairest allocation of funds of this sort in very complex and frequently competing fields.
Hon. members will realize that the budget of the Medical Research Council has received continuous increasing support, and I hope this will be so in the future. I have indicated in dollars the share of the total research funds for medical research which passed through the Medical Research Council.
I would like to say that the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Athabasca was rather harsh in his judgment not only of the government's motivation but also of its actions. I hope that shortly, perhaps this weekend, he will be able to return to his native province and invite Albertans, as the government of Alberta has indicated it will do, to participate in a substantial grant through the Heritage fund to cancer research. I have not included this prospective large sum of money in the figures I have quoted because so far the government of Alberta has only indicated an interest, rather than a firm intention, in undertaking this funding. I think the hon. member for Athabasca would be pleased if the government of Alberta were to come through with funds for this very worth-while cause.
The hon. member offered some suggestions as to how the system of funding could be improved. One of his suggestions was that more money should be allocated. That is an easy answer, but at a time of limited funds for all federal as well as provincial government operations, more money is no answer at all; it is merely a form of escapism. However, I suggest that one of the problems in relation to the council was what he called the stop-and-go nature of the grants, the uncertainty among the recipients as to how much money will be granted and for how long they might receive it.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has recognized this problem, and perhaps the hon. member for Athabasca got this idea from the minister himself at a committee meeting when the minister indicated that work was going forward within his department to try to see if grants by the council could not be reorganized to provide more certainty of continuity than perhaps has been the case in the past. Improvements could be made in this area even without additional funds. Certainly the Minister of National Health and Welfare and I support this kind of initiative.
The hon. member for Athabasca suggested that we should catch up with both the U.S. and Sweden in the area of medical research. Perhaps this is desirable in terms of giving ourselves a glow of well-being, but given the fact, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pointed out as recently as this morning, that we are in the situation of trying to consume more in a year than we are able or willing to produce-

Consequently, we are in the process now of having to make selections between what we can do and what we cannot do, what we want to do and what we want not to do. In the case of medical research, case histories have been read out to the House. This could go on forever. The list of human ailments is almost without end, and the list of people who would be interested in pursuing cures for them is also very large indeed. The fact of the matter is that we as a country cannot afford to undertake all the research that requires to be done, given the limited resources both in people and in money that we have available for this purpose. Selections have to be made and the method of making these selections in this area is through the granting councils.
It has been suggested that the Medical Research Council has been denied the amount of money that they need in the current year to keep up with their level of operations in the previous year. I am told that the advice was given to the Minister of National Health and Welfare some months ago that in order to maintain the November, 1975, level of activity in the current year an additional sum of $1.2 million would be needed. The minister was able to find in his departmental budget, from other prospective activities, the sum of $2 million which was allocated to the Medical Research Council, so that the allegation that the council does not have sufficient funds this year to keep with last year's activities is demonstrably unfounded. Indeed, more money than the minimum they said was needed has been furnished to the council.
This is not, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare has said on a number of occasions, as much of national resources going through the Medical Research Council for medical research as we would like to see. To be quite frank, this is not as much as I would like to see. One hopes that with the intention of the government to reorganize the three granting councils-which, unfortunately, given our legislative timetable, is not possible before June 30, which, however, with the co-operation of the opposition I hope we will be able to process through the legislative machine next fall-the cause of research will be better served.
With that legislation, the prospects for the new science and engineering council, the humanities and social science council and the Medical Research Council working closer together to adequately serve the cause of research in the universities will be much better than at the moment.
The hon. member for Athabasca indicated, rather loosely I felt, that the cause of research in Canada was "totally neglected", to use his words, by the government. I would suggest that in the case of medical research, continuous real growth, after discounting inflation over the period of the seven years 1 have sketched, does not correspond to total neglect. Like so many other things, I have indicated it is not as much and as often as a number of us would like, of course. Those who are worried about the lack of investment, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg
Medical Research
North Centre (Mr. Knowles), should remember that in the current year we are operating within a framework of rather severely limited resources, but this does not represent a cutback in any sense of the term.
The hon. member for Athabasca made one statement which I should like flatly to contradict. On the strength of some rather dubious arithmetic he indicated that proportionately more researchers were leaving Canada for the United States than were coming here, and that we as a country are providing the training for them at our cost and thus are the net losers. I am advised that from July 1, 1974, to June 30, 1975, 24 Canadian researchers went to the United States and 58 came from the United States to Canada, a net gain of around 100 per cent of the Canadian movement. This is not simply an isolated phenomenon peculiar to this one year, but is a trend that has been persistent for the last few years. Those who try to bolster a weak case with this kind of phony endeavour to frighten people weaken what is a good cause by trying to support it with fallacies.
The hon. member for Athabasca also indicated that I said somewhere, sometime, that we should depend on the United States for our research. I am not sure of his exact words, but they are so foreign to my notion of what it should be that I could not quite catch them.

Mr. Speaker, I must initially compliment the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) for introducing the motion condemning the government's lack of support for medical research in Canada and outlining deficiencies in the government's program for sustaining a viable medical research community.
I am glad to see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) back in the House.
I have not been away.

I was surprised to hear him say almost in his opening comments that the NDP is as concerned, perhaps more concerned, about medical research as is my party. I noticed that the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) conveniently managed to defuse this afternoon's debate which, basically, has to do with medical research in Canada. He used arguments which have been used in the past. Although he spoke of funds for research being available from provincial sources, federal sources, and private individuals, it is important to remember that today we are debating the federal government's direct responsibility in medical research.
Since my first election in 1972 to the House of Commons the issue of adequate funding for medical research has been a recurrent theme. The biomedical research community has limped from one financial crisis to another. We have seen a reduction in the spending of constant dollars, a termination of programs of excellence, a rejection of projects submitted by highly qualified scientists, the introduction of disincentives which do not entice able young men and women to take up research careers, and a lack of long term fiscal policies to ensure stability and responsible growth in the research community.
If one were to examine all speeches made in this House since I became a member, examine testimony presented before the standing committee, look carefully at the annual reports of the Medical Research Council, assess the great volume of correspondence members have received on this subject, and read the editorials and reports in newspapers on this subject, one point above all would become obvious, that is that the federal government has been and is pre-
