If one compares the moneys required to sustain a constant and steady growth in the research committed vis-avis the money committed to a variety of other government programs during my four years in this House of Commons, it must lead one to ask why the continued disinterest by the government in biomedical research. Its propensity for spending in recent years, and I understand there is a projected increase of 16 per cent for this coming year, makes a mockery out of the statement that it cannot find an additional $2 million or $3 million for this present fiscal year.
Why has the government refused to develop a long-term policy to ensure the stability of this very significant component of our health care system? Surely strategy that would ensure the future health of our most important resource, people, should receive the same attention as the government attempt to develop an energy policy, which I remind hon. members for the most part is a non-renewable resource.
The answers to these questions are by no means clear. However, I think it is worth noting that an unprecedented dissection of the health care system has occurred since the introduction of the Hospital and Diagnostic Services Act and medicare. I believe it is the rapidly escalating cost of medical care and not health that has precipitated the debate as to how the health professions function today. I want to emphasize that. It is the escalating cost of medicare and not health which has really precipitated this debate.
The preoccupation with health care costs has produced an endless stream of reports frequently suggesting oversimplistic solutions to solve a very complex problem. Indeed, it has become fashionable in recent years to become an instant expert with ready made solutions. The least that can be said for these well meaning individuals is their uniformity in failing to resolve the shortcomings in the health system with their suggestions.
I do not for a moment under emphasize the importance of escalating health costs, and indeed there is ample evidence to substantiate that the consumer cost of hospital care has risen rapidly and that furthermore, contrary to the impressions created by the government, the costs continue to be unevenly and inequitably distributed.
The reasons for the rising costs are many. Some are understandable, justifiable, and inevitable. In many instances the rising costs of certain kinds of medical care have often been presented in highly misleading ways that do not take into account the changes in the sophistication of services offered. For example, to compare the cost of treatment for a heart attack 15 years ago with what it costs
95570-19%

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
to treat the same illness today in a coronary care unit is like comparing the cost of a Model T Ford and the cost of a Concorde jetliner just because both represent a vehicle of transportation.
The ongoing debate in the search for alternate forms of delivery of health care to ensure the services of the right kind, at the right time, to the right person, has propelled us into the era of consumerism.
I have not sensed major objections to assessing the shortcomings to our health care system and to developing tools for measuring the quality of care rendered both in and out of hospital.
During this period of self-examination and social analysis, which is characteristic of any society or problem plagued by unrest and uncertainty, the government has seen the failure of its social programs to correct internal problems and yet is reticent to admit these failures. Health care has not escaped this examination.
The government, in my view, has not recognized the complexities of the problems, and because the basic issues do not fit into convenient and conventional economic and political pigeonholes they are interpreted as being insolu-able, with the predictable consequences of inaction, overreaction, or the introduction of simplistic solutions. Biomedical research has been one of the victims of this mentality.
I believe it is fair to say that during the forties and fifties there was a simplistic belief that unlimited funds put into biomedical research would produce instant understanding of disease entities that would be transferred immediately to the market place and to the consumer. During my post graduate years in Washington, D.C., this Alice in Wonderland attiteude was expressed by the presence of such institutions as the National Institute of Health. Notwithstanding the gains in knowledge and major accomplishments of biomedical research which I will refer to in a moment, this unrealistic attitude which was never fostered by the scientific community at that time or today resulted in unrealistic expectations which have overshadowed monumental accomplishments. I have sensed this attitude is present in the government and has been interpreted by the government as a failure of the research community to resolve complex health problems which, unfortunately, have permeated its thinking with the resultant effect that biomedical research has been designated as a non-priority item.
It should be noted in passing that the government has an unmistakable loss of confidence in the value and effectiveness of science. It touches science in general, and medicine in particular. I was glad that the Minister of State for Science and Technology was here today because we talked about this recently on an opposition day where science in general was the focal point of that particular debate.
The government, in its inability to grasp the complexities of the problem, has sown the seeds of doubt about the capacity of science to solve our health problems. The doubt generated by the government has not unexpectedly generated intense public anxiety, and genuine fears have suddenly been replaced by acupuncture, copper bracelets, transcendental meditation, or astrology.

The question can be logically asked what has transpired in recent years to generate such criticism of our health care system? Why is it fashionable for so many to say there is nothing good in the system? I believe the answer to that question, at least in part, is related to the misunderstanding of technology, and not economics, as suggested by the government.
How many in this Chamber recall when our hospitals were filled with lobar pneumonia, when meningococal meningitis and scarlet fever took their annual toll, when outbreaks of diptheria would plague urban centres, when typhoid fever and erysipilas would cause fear and panic at the mere mention of the word? With the introduction of sulfanamides, penicillin, streptomycin, and other antibiotics a revolution in hospital care evolved, unprecedented in history.
Can you visualize the problems in hospital financing today if all the subsequent changes that have occurred, including hospital insurance, had not been accompanied by the technology to control major infectious diseases? It is important for each of us to recall this bit of history since it has and will repeat itself in the future if we continue to get results to which we are entitled from the biomedical research community.
The point which must be emphasized, and which the government has not grasped, is that the future of hospital economies is clearly bound up with the future of medical science and technology. In this I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Dr. Lewis Thomas, president of the Memorial Sloan-Ket-tering Cancer Centre in New York, and professor of Pathology and Medicine at the Cornell University College of Medicine, has defined three quite different levels of technology in medicine so unlike each other that practitioners of medicine and the analysts of our system will be in trouble if the differences are not understood and kept separate.
First there is the large body of what he termed "nontechnology". This is impossible to measure in terms of its capacity to alter either the natural course of disease or its eventual outcome. A great deal of money is spent on this, and it is highly valued by the professionals as well as by the patients. It consists of what is commonly called supportive therapy and includes what physicians must now do for patients with intractable cancer, severe rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, strokes, and advanced cirrhosis, to name but a few. The cost of this non-technology is very high and getting higher all the time. It represents the efforts not only of a substantial segment of the health professionals in coping with this kind of problem but obviously represents a substantial segment of the health sector.
The second form of technology defined by Dr. Thomas is termed "half-way technology". This represents the kind of actions which must be taken after the fact to compensate for the incapacitating effects of certain diseases. It is a technology designed to make up for disease or to postpone death. Examples in recent years are transplantations of hearts, kidneys, livers, other organs, and the invention of artificial organs. In the public mind this kind of technolo-
June 15, 1976

gy has come to appear as the equivalent of the high technology of the physical sciences.
The media tends to present each new procedure as though it constituted a break-through or a therapeutic triumph, instead of being the make-shift it really is. This type of technology is at times, by its very nature, highly sophisticated. Yet it is still primitive. It is the sort of thing one must do until there is a general understanding of the mechanisms involved in disease. Such technology, embracing as it does the development of costly apparatus to manage heart attacks, specialized ambulances, distinct hospital units, and electronic gadgetry is characterized by the necessity of investing enormous sums of money in hospitals, hospital facilities, and highly trained people. This portion of medicine will be with us in the future and our only hope of removing this level of technology lies in the new information which can be obtained through research.
The third kind of technology which is described by Dr. Thomas is the kind which is so effective that it seems to attract the least public notice; it is the kind which is taken for granted. I referred previously to the revolution in hospital care which came about with the introduction of antibiotics and modern methods of immunization against diphtheria, whooping cough, and childhood virus diseases. Our capability in dealing with tuberculosis and syphilis was a major medical triumph despite the fact that, in my view, full use has never been made of this potential. The treatment of endocrinologic disorders with appropriate hormones following basic research in immunology in Liverpool, England, is now virtually wiping out hemalytic disease of the new-born which occurs in Rh-negative mothers. There are other examples, but the truth is there are not as many as the public has been led to believe.
The point to emphasize about this kind of technology, one which implies a genuine understanding of disease mechanisms, is that when it becomes available it is relatively inexpensive, relatively simple, and relatively easy to deliver.
I refer to the influence that the discovery of antibiotics had on medical care. If a case of typhoid fever had to be managed today by the best methods of the mid-thirties, the expense would be staggering. Counting about 56 days of hospitalization during which demanding standards of nursing care would be required, careful dietary consideration, constant laboratory monitoring, and surgical intervention in certain circumstances, a conservative estimate of the cost of the illness would be around $10,000 in today's terms. The cost today would be a bottle of cloramphenical and a day or two of fever.

Would the hon. member accept a question? Would he acknowledge that many of the discoveries he has mentioned, particularly in the field of antibiotics, were the result of accidents such as in the celebrated case of Dr. Fleming's discovery of penicillin? Or would he not agree they were discoveries in the private sector, particularly within the pharmaceutical industry, rather than the results of long-term and expensive research at the universities?

The question is only partly pertinent. I was attempting to make the point that biomedical research,
Medical Research
whether in the universities or in the private sector, has been responsible for the major break-throughs we have seen.
The hon. member for Athabasca referred earlier to the statement by Dr. Fudenberg before a sub-committee in the United States about a year ago. This statement gave evidence of other areas in which large savings had been made as a result of discovery in the course of research into immunology. The point I wish to emphasize is that it is the responsibility of the federal government to ensure that this basic research is carried on in an acceptable fashion.
I want to say a word now about target research, or applied research. Although there is general agreement that applied research should be encouraged in certain key areas I believe it would be an error to do this at the expense of basic research or by restricting the freedom of our scientists. If freedom is severely curtailed, scientists will lose their enthusiasm and become less productive or, more tragic still, move to a country where greater freedom exists.
Traditionally the major function of a university is to teach and generate new knowledge through research. In my opinion it would be tragic if research priorities were established by government, as suggested in the Speech from the Throne and subsequent statements by the former minister responsible for science and technology, thereby placing the major burden of applied research on the universities. I do not suggest that applied research cannot be structured into such institutes, and indeed there are examples of successful endeavours in this respect. However, it should be noted that universities are involved in important tasks in connection with higher education and the development of new knowledge. In existing circumstances it seems unreasonable to ask the universities to maintain high standards of performance while accepting new responsibilities for government-directed research.

I thank the House for permitting me a few more moments in which to speak. I shall try to summarize. I only wish I had more time to give a detailed account of the many problems which are presently facing the research community. However, it is my personal belief that future action in the medical research community is really predicated upon an understanding of the basic importance and the problems of medical research. I hope that in the very brief time that I have taken this afternoon I have persuaded the Minister of State for Science and Technology and the government of the importance of this particular sector of technology, and I have attempted to define technology as I see it and as viewed by many. I Rope the government will develop a long-term policy to restore confidence to this important segment of our health care system.

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
I should like to conclude by quoting an article entitled "The Technology of Medicine" by Dr. Lewis Thomas which appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1971. He concluded the article with the following observation:
It is when physicians are bogged down by their incomplete technologies, by the innumerable things they are obliged to do in medicine, when they lack a clear understanding of disease mechanisms, that the deficiencies of the health care system are most conspicuous. If I were a policy maker interested in saving money for health care over the long haul, I would regard it as an act of high prudence to give high priority to a lot more basic research in biologic science. This is the only way to get the full mileage that biology owes to the science of medicine, even though it seems, as used to be said in the days when the phase still had some meaning, like asking for the moon.
One can only hope that the minister, who has been present today, and the government will grasp the implications of this very famous physician's observations.

Mr. Speaker, we are faced today with a motion of the opposition which describes very well, in my mind, how the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Yewchuk) sees his role as a parliamentarian either in this House or in standing committees. I could elaborate further in a moment if the hon. member wants to be patient.
I would like to say, however, that I am not against medical research nor am I opposed to basic medical research financing in Canada. First of all, I would like to mention that I have enough scars on my whole body to say how much I appreciate the advancement of sciences which have enabled me to recover my health.
It is however obvious for anyone who has read the text of this motion put forward today that it is filled with partisan views, that it is basically negative and reflects failure of its sponsor to propose valuable and responsible solutions and to advocate some kind of alternatives.
And how easy it is with a subject like this one which receives the support of the majority of Canadians, I am not afraid to say so, how easy it is to indulge in demagogy! Obviously, any objective individual who has followed the development of medical research funding in recent years will admit with me that the achievements of this government are certainly not as described by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) or his colleagues.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), through his positive attitude, his availability, his flexibility, his wish to engage in a dialogue thas will lead to new cooperation avenues does much more for Canada, for the welfare of Canadians, for medical research than the individuals who see only the bad side of the situation and live in isolation without any regard for other sectors of the Canadian economy.
I referred a moment ago to the open-mindedness of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and to his will to cooperate. As evidence I wish to quote some of his remarks made before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on May 18. This is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) said:
With regard to medical research, once more-and I have said so-I felt that the increase was inadequate. Even with the additional $2 million-
And here the minister refers to the announcement made the same night about the $2 million increase in the medical research budget which he took from elsewhere in his department. I think it is satisfying evidence of his good will and his good intentions. I continue the quotation and it is still the minister who is speaking:
-I am not boasting that we are really rushing ahead and putting money into medical research. It is just going to allow medical research to keep up, roughly with where it was last November. It is nothing to boast of, in the sense, as I said, that we are just a country being over generous.
So, Mr. Speaker, the minister is frank and sincere beyond reproach.
I go on reading his comments, and I draw here the attention of the author of today's motion to the following passage, hoping he will see in it not illogical and irresponsible decisions, as he says, but a sense of organisation and planning. I quote:
But, once more, you have to look at it in a longer perspective than that of one or two years. You have to realize that over the last decade we have put a relatively high priority on the total funding of medical research.
And to support what the minister was saying in 1966-67, the budget of the Medical Research Coucil was $12,350,000 and for the current fiscal year, it has been increased to $50 million, Mr. Speaker.
I think what we should be looking at over the next few years, and what I am most concerned about in medical research, is those fluctuations, those cycles in medical research. I think this is most unfortunate. One year you get an 18-per cent increase, the next year you get 2 per cent. As you yourself, or as some of your colleagues, have said ...
... he was speaking to a member of the committee, Dr. Halliday .. .
You cannot just turn it on and off as if it were a water tap. What we are trying to develop is a kind of formula or criterion, by which research . .. particularly medical research .. . will be able to count on some reasonably steady rate of growth in its expenditures.
I have argued with some people saying, even if we were to say 5 per cent a year or 3 per cent a year, at least we would know what to expect, and the researchers would know what to expect. Those who found it not good enough would leave, abandon, or do something else, but at least there would be some direction. I hope it will be higher than that, and that it will be related to some other criterion.
I think one of the big problems we are facing in medical research, and research generally, is the establishment of some criterion upon which researchers will be able to plan on the basis of a longer term than in the past, and I hope we will be able to arrive at that this year.
Mr Speaker, I apologize for quoting in full such a lengthy extract from the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, but I think it was important today, in the absence of the minister, to record his views so that Canadians will know exactly that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is a righteous and honest man devoted to the welfare of all Canadians.
What I find most encouraging, Mr. Speaker, in this whole matter, is the will to co-operate that we seem to have suddenly discovered. On the one hand, we have the medical research community which says it needs more money for the current fiscal year, to which the minister replied by a $2 million increase, and on the other hand, federal restraints are now being felt in every field. It will

June 15, 1976

be remembered that on December 18 last, the President of the Treasury Board, the Hon. Jean Chretien announced the action taken by the government under its anti-inflation program.
The Medical Research Council was not the only one affected by this action, but the fact remains that at that time, the President of the Treasury Board, while admitting the restraints, still allowed a budgetary increase of $1 million, plus $414,000 which were transfered to the Department of National Health and Welfare from the Department of Veterans Affairs, and this was in addition to the $2 million announced last month. This is therefore a rather large increase when we know that other departments were not as lucky.

On the long term, I mentioned some of the issues in terms of maintaining stability, including consideration and careful monitoring of the costs of research which is being done now, including setting new directions by the MRC in terms of new programs or changing their programs in terms of looking at the schools that have special needs that need to be developed. I think these are some of the categories to look into. We have proposed to the minister that perhaps a meeting of interested people in government, political parties-
I have some doubts about this-
-.scientists, and MRC be held to discuss in greater detail the issue of long-term funding. I hope that will come to fruition.
In fact, we all know now that these meetings have started and that they will go on during the summer, which is to the credit of all people of good will who do not simply criticize, as the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Yewchuk) usually does, but who unceasingly and conscientiously work at a very complex problem in a society which is always asking and demanding more from its governments.
As far as catching up is concerned, and particularly in the field of medical research, it is suggested that a per capita contribution similar to that in the United States or Western Germany would be a good thing for Canada. This is maybe a commendable aim but it is a bit too simplistic. As I said in the beginning, this is like living in isolation. Even if we admit this relative progress by those countries, it remains that they have some catching up to do with our policies here in Canada and with our financial support for social programs such as medicare, hospital insurance and the many social programs which I will not enumerate here but which are all familiar to us and which excite the envy of many other countries, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said today during question period.
Medical Research
I shall not drag on refuting more than necessary today's motion. Several colleagues want to take the floor and they are perfectly able to come to grips with that question but I am obliged to recognize that, on top of being essentially negative, the motion is pessimistic and it does not take into account all that has been done for some time to promote a dialogue between the scientific community, the government, the Medical Research Council and-why not-the politicians in senior positions.
I shall end by quoting, as I have done during my remarks, the minutes of proceedings of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. I have to quote myself to put the question in its true context. During the Friday May 28 meeting of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, where Dr. J. Gordon Kaplan, President of the Canadian Federation of Biological Studies was one of the witnesses, I asked the following question:
Is it not true that we have reached this critical threshold of readiness of mind and of practical and open dialogue?
Dr. Kaplan answered:
It is true that the dialogues have started. I must add that it already existed between the hon. Health Minister and the medical research community of Canada.
For the past two or three years, his door has always been open to us and we have been able to talk frankly with him, although you know what consequences this may have: unfortunately, an open dialogue does not guarantee that medical researchers will have enough funds. Nevertheless, I agree with your optimism and we hope that this true dialogue will lead to the development of a long-term policy on medical research subsidization.
And why put all the burden on the government, Mr. Speaker? It seems to me that the medical community has, too, the responsibility and duty to plan its own research, to establish its own priorities and not to rely always on the government.
It is obvious, from the statements I quoted today, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the medical research community, including the Medical Research Council, are much more optimistic than the hon. member for Athabasca and his party as regards the future. That is why I cannot support this motion. I feel the remarks of the hon. member for Athabasca add nothing of substance to the debate, and that the minister has already taken into account all the representations made in committee of the House. An attempt was made to politicize a problem which, to my mind, is now in the process of being solved.
The doctors and medical researchers lobby is possibly the best organized and among the most powerful in the land; to my mind, it was not necessary to draw the attention of the House to this matter today. As for me, Mr. Speaker, I come from an underdeveloped area of the country, which is often badly developed. I should have thought that on the Progressive Conservative side the hon. members would have preferred taking up the matter of regional disparities, of equal opportunities, instead of rehashing the same old arguments in a lobby that it is quite capable of taking care of its own needs, which indeed it has proved very ably.

I just cannot be turned on by today's motion and the plea for more medical research funds in the way the motion is

worded. After listening to all opposition spokesmen I am more than ever convinced that the object of today's debate was to try to score political points against the government, and not so much a concern for the benefit of the medical research community in Canada.
Hear, hear!

That is not to say, and I would like to repeat, that I am against medical research. I am for medical research for the same reason I am for motherhood, for fatherhood, or the sacred cows of India, or democracy. The real question is whether or not the government is administering the public moneys in a responsible and balanced way. I believe it is. The question really is a matter of balance, balance of job creation, equal opportunity throughout all areas of the country and a happy life, and balanced growth in all departmental expenditures.
In conclusion may I say I am surprised that such a motion would come forward today from the hon. member for Athabasca after the poor show we went through on Friday a week ago when this House had referred back to it from the standing committee a bill to control smoking in public transit facilities. The committee spent something like six full meetings debating the question. In the course of those meetings it was proven that smoking is obnoxious to non-smokers. Money was spent on interpreters, on printers, and on other salaries in respect of the committee. The committee referred the bill back to this House in a modified form. Who opposed the measure to improve the health of Canadians? None other than the hon. member for Athabasca, and that is a bloody shame!

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member has just terminated his speech with what comes closest to the unusable term. He told an untruth at the conclusion of his speech. If he had bothered to listen to or read what I said in the committee or in the House when that bill came back, he would know that I supported the bill all the way. He should withdraw that falsehood. It is unacceptable. The bill was spoken to by five members, including members from the other side, during that hour of debate, and they must take just as much blame as we do for the bill not having passed at that time. I think the hon. member should withdraw that falsehood.

I will be fair with the member from Athabasca. It is quite possible he did not understand the way I put the question. He may not have been opposed to the legislation, but he certainly organized the blocking of the passage of that legislation in the House.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, before we recessed for dinner tonight we heard the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) launch into what might be called a tirade not on the subject of our debate today but rather on the matter of the provision of separate accommodation for smoking in public conveyances. Therefore I think it might be apropos to review what the motion before the House today is. It reads as follows:
That this House views with great alarm the ill-considered and illogical decisions of the government which fail to give adequate priority to health research funding.
We are talking about research, Mr. Speaker, not about a bill which was before the House some time ago.
I want to approach the subject for debate today from two or three aspects that are somewhat unnconventional and different from what we have heard of late. First, I want to allude briefly to some of the peculiar attitudes of the government toward research. Second, I would like to touch on some of the philosophies behind health care research which do not seem to be understood by the government. Third, I want to speak about aspects of medical research to which adequate consideration has not been given by the speakers from whom we have heard so far in this debate in
June 15, 1976

the House or in the committee, namely, research into the practice of family medicine, a very important part of the health care delivery system in Canada.
First of all I should like to get rid of some rather unpleasant comments which I feel I must make about the govenment's approach to the subject of medical research in the last year or so. It was disappointing to me when it was brought to my attention by some people from the research community who were on Parliament Hill in the last month or two that they received a very discourteous and unfriendly reception from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) when they visited him in his office not long ago. That does not get any marks for the government or for the whole principle of medical research.
The second point which concerns me has been alluded to by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) when he led off very capably for the official opposition, and that is that there has been an obvious lack of attendance by some important members of the government who should be here. I am the first to admit that reasons were given why the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his parliamentary secretary could not be here, and I accept them. I presume the same is the case for the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien). However, it is gratifying to see here tonight the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) because he, like the Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Drury), comes from a community in Canada where there is much interest in medical research. I am surprised that those two ministers have not been able to come up with a more effective program for the provision of research funds in view of the local interest which exists in their communities.
There is a third matter that concerns me regarding actions of the government. It relates to what has gone on in the Department of National Health and Welfare in the past and up to the present. I want to raise one particular instance and I hope I will not offend anyone. It has been brought to my attention that Dr. Jack Wiggin, who was employed in the Department of National Health and Welfare as head of the health research grant program until about the end of 1975, had a very difficult time as head of that branch. His role was to assess and rule on grant applications which came before the department. As most hon. members know, these grants are scrutinized by at least three separate committees. One was a committee of the department itself, another was a committee of outside experts, and there was a third committee, all of which could offer opinions on grant applications.
There is one glaring example of where an application was made for a grant, was approved by all three committees, and it had to be vetoed by a man higher in the department than the director of the branch itself. That was so deplorable that the committee threatened to resign and the chairman of this branch has since resigned. That is the kind of department that tries to run the program of research grants in this country, and it is disappointing to learn of it.
Recently a well known medical educator in this country told me how disappointed he was with the status of the staff in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Medical Research
He said it has gradually gone down hill in the last five or six years and that he could count on one hand five competent people in the department now as compared to the situation some years ago.
Dealing with the attitude of the government, there is one other area to which I should like to allude and which has been discussed in some detail by other members. It concerns the spending attitude of the government as it relates to medical research. I can summarize this whole thing rather succinctly in a quotation from an article by Dr. Daniel H. Osmond, Associate Professor in the Departments of Physiology and Medicine at the University of Toronto. I will quote from the article which appeared in the spring edition of The Graduate, a publication of the University of Toronto. He was referring to the feelings of research workers after the announcement last December of the freeze on research grants. The article was headed "Sickness in Canada's Health System" and he wrote:
This much was clear: the financial noose was firmly in place. Inflation would steadily complete the strangulation.
That is the attitude and feeling of research people across the country toward the government's conduct of medical research.
While discussing the peculiar attitude of the government I should like to touch on something to ward off an obvious argument the government has brought forth in committee on many occasions about recommendations from the official opposition to the effect that there should be an increase in spending in certain areas. We are always told that we cannot have it both ways.
I was very interested to read an article not too long ago in a magazine called Farm and Country, which is circulated to 86,000 farmers across Canada. It is a lay organization as far as medical research is concerned and as far as the costs of health care are concerned. The government tries to tell us that we must follow a policy of restraint and that the only way to do it is its way. But, Mr. Speaker, there are other ways of looking at it. I have been upset when this point has been brought up with the Minister of National Health and Welfare and he has just replied that we are not going to have any deterrents, as though there is something bad about the word. I do not like the word myself, but he is using it in the wrong sense. When we use it on this side of the House we mean to stop the over-use and abuse of the health care system. If the minister would look at it that way he could find ways to save the extra money that the research people need.
The editorial in Farm and Country of May 25, 1976, dealt with the closing of the hospital in Chesley. It is a layman speaking on behalf of farm and country people. It reads:
It gives us little satisfaction to note that five years ago we predicted that neither Ontario nor Canada could afford a lavish health system. At that time we pointed out that comprehensive medicare was bankrupting Britain, and the same would happen in Canada. Politicians of all parties, who fostered the something-for-nothing attitude among the electorate, must share the blame for the present crisis.
Apart from that perhaps negative approach to the problem, the editorial advanced three rather constructive suggestions which I would recommend to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. One comes from the chairman of the Chesley and District Memorial Hospital board
14538

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
who suggests a fee of $4 per day for people using the hospital.
Another suggestion comes from one of the board members of the same hospital who thinks that patients, who are able to, could pay $100 per year for their health care bill. This, if applied nationally, would save hundreds of millions of dollars which could be applied to medical research. He also suggested-and he is talking about OHIP because he happens to be in Ontario but this would apply to any government-sponsored health care plan-that in the area of cost cutting there could be a new approach to billing OHIP. He says that when patients visit a physician's office they never see the amount the government run service is charged for the consultation or treatment.
I can suggest a fourth way in which the minister could save money for medical research. The patients could pay the physician directly and then collect the money from the appropriate source, be it the government or a private plan. The government could save money in many areas but it pretends the only way it can do it is by cutting back on the funds available for medical research.
Going on to deal with some of the problems of the philosophy of the government in regard to medical research, I should like to read a quotation from the magazine I referred to earlier, The Graduate. The article entitled "Sickness in Canada's Health System" by Dr. Osmond reads as follows:
"For the first time in 20 years," says one head of a medical science department in Toronto, "I would advise graduate students to leave Canada."
There is a problem in medical research funding no matter what the Minister of State for Science and Technology says, or what the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria says, or how they try to juggle the figures to prove it is not so. It is obvious there is a problem, and the system is being down-graded because of lack of funds.
Another area which is certainly very important and is often not recognized as being a problem is that the Minister of State for Science and Technology does not understand what medical research and health care are all about. To go back to the article I just quoted from, it reports Dr. Malcolm Brown, President of the Medical Research Council, an agency of the Department of National Health and Welfare, as saying:
The effect of research on the quality of teaching and on patient care is evident in the ways in which patients seek out teaching hospitals for treatment. The evidence supports the view that there is a positive relation between the amount of research, the quality of teaching, and the amount learned.
The Department of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of State for Science and Technology do not seem to appreciate the fact that there is a close connection between research, teaching medicine, and the quality of health care, and that any restraint in expenditures in these areas is going to affect adversely medical teaching and thus the quality of care which Canadians receive.
I should like now to discuss two areas which come under the heading of the concepts or philosophies of research and health care. There must be a distinction between research and development. We hear a lot about "R & D" which is carried out by many government departments at the present time. Of course research is something entirely

different from development. Research is something you spend money on without knowing exactly where you are going and what the results will be. Development is where you spend money on a program that you know is going to achieve a certain result. Unfortunately our government does not appreciate the distinction between the areas of research and development. Because of the long term implications it seems unwilling to spend money on research. It would rather spend money in the area of development.
We must also consider the problem of in-house research, a new term which connotes the concept that research should be carried on by people in the Department of National Health and Welfare. The researchers who have been on Parliament Hill during the last few weeks have brought to our attention a deplorable situation. Apparently in the most recent spending estimates there is to be a 16 per cent increase in moneys allotted for "in-house" spending. That represents a considerable sum.
While on this topic may I quote from page 94 of report No. 22 of the Science Council of Canada, entitled "Science for Health Services", dated October, 1974. A note of dissent was sounded by M. Bonneau, a well-known health care worker and educator in Quebec. Speaking about in-house research he said, as the report notes on page 94:
... Judgments on the scientific quality of the researcher and his project can be made only by experienced people, capable of understanding the objective and evaluating the correlation between the means and the end.
... Any structure for the encouragement and co-ordination of research efforts must be removed as fast as possible from the administrative and political area.
I submit that we should curtail in-house medical research and allow experts in the field to conduct such research.
I am concerned about the government's lack of consistency in medical research spending. In this regard I wish to quote Pavlov. As hon. members know, Pavlov left the world a legacy in the field of the conditioned reflex. In a message to youth he said:
What would I wish for the young people of my motherland who dedicated themselves to science? First of all-consistency .. . Consistency, consistency and again consistency ... Inculcate in yourself the habit of strict consistency in acquiring knowledge ... Restraint and patience ... Modesty... Do not let pride take possession of you ... Be passionate in your work and in your quests.
I suggest that the medical researchers of this country have been patient, have been consistent and, above all, have been passionate in their work. They passionately plead for more money for medical research.
In my remaining few minutes I wish to touch on the important subject of research related to the practice of family medicine. I have some experience in this area. In Canada health care in the majority of cases for the majority of people is delivered by the family physician. It is about time we spent more on research relating to the practice of family medicine. The previously alluded to report of the Science Council of Canada touches on this subject at page 82. Under the heading "Adequacy of Funding", we read the following:
June 15, 1976

The R & D on health care delivery ... is less than half the above amount.
The author is referring to the fact, alluded to in the previous sentence, that Canada spends 1 per cent of the costs of health care on R & D in health services. I continue quoting:
Such a low level is inconsistent with sound industrial practice. An increase in the small outlay on health care R & D is obviously needed to improve the value obtained from the much larger outlay (over 200 times) on health care itself.
The report lists a number of government departments and various other agencies which spend money on R & D. The Department on National Health and Welfare ranks ninth on that list.
The report goes on to say:
It is not an impressive illustration of the relative importance currently being attached to health care R & D. This would be of little significance if the needs for new knowledge in this field were reasonably well satisfied. However, the preceding pages should have shown that the extent of the outstanding need for knowledge is such that it will have little chance of being met without a major increase in funding.
The foregoing illustrates why we should spend much more on medical research and on research in family medicine. We could examine many areas of family practice. Time does not permit me to deal with them. I will do this on another occasion when I can put facts in more detail before the House.
May I now draw to the attention of the House some comments made by Dr. Donald I. Rice, executive director of the College of Family Physicians of Canada, at the national conference on research in family practice held in Miami, Florida, in January, 1975. He said in part:
The appropriate funding of family practice research is a must if we are to encourage an adequate number of researchers to become involved in research activity. Research costs money as well as time, and we must do what we can to find the necessary funds to support legitimate investigations in family practice. Here the practising family doctor interested in research is at a distinct disadvantage vis-a-vis his confrere with an academic appointment.
He went on to say-
Order, please. I must interrupt the hon. member to inform his that his allotted time has expired. He may continue if he has unanimous consent. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent to continue?
Agreed.

I thank hon. members for their indulgence.
I shall speak only a few more sentences. Dr. Rice went on to say:
Major funding bodies must accept that family practice research will play an increasingly important part in determining the future direction of health care in our respective countries, and they must be encouraged to invest the necessary research money to ensure that adequate numbers of family physician researchers are being trained, and that appropriate investigations are being carried out.
Finally, I cannot do better than quote Hippocrates, known as the father of modern medicine. He said, in about 400 BC:
Other discoveries will yet be found out, if a person possessed of the proper ability, and knowing those discoveries which have been made, should proceed from them-to prosecute his own investigations.
Medical Research
Following the words of Hippocrates, Canadian researchers will be unable to prosecute their investigations unless the government reconsiders the provision of medical research funding.

Mr. Speaker, for the second time in two years I participate in debate on this subject. I think the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk) told the House he has participated in similar debates three times. I hope that we shall not participate in any more such debates for some time, considering how this debate has been carried on. I cannot help but agree with the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) that this debate has been disappointing, to say the least.
What has been disappointing?

The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is not here; his parliamentary secretary is not here, and the Conservative spokesman, the hon. member for Athabasca, could not be here himself this afternoon. Worse than that, throughout the afternoon attendance in this House was poor.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I point out that I was here all this afternoon, except for one hour when I went out to attend my daughter's graduation.
Hear, hear!
Apologize. Withdraw.
According to my recollection, there was, generally, poor attendance this afternoon on the part of members of the official opposition party. Sometimes fewer than five were present.
Fewer than five!
The same goes for the other opposition party, the NDP.
If that is a demonstration on your debating skill, you can quit now.

At one time the hon. member for Athabasca spoke of heart attacks. As he said, we do not want any member of this House to have a heart attack. You know, we could translate the work of researchers into concrete results if we work at it. For example, the pamphlet put out at the initiative of the Minister of National Health and Welfare having to do with a new perspective on the health of Canadians deals with physical fitness and how physical fitness can prevent heart attacks. I wonder how many of the hon. member's colleagues have lately used our gym facilities to improve their own physical fitness. It is not just research that is important. It is using the results of research as well.

Oh, oh!
95570-20/4

June 15, 1976
Medical Research

I ask the opposition to accord our speakers the same kind of respect and silence that we accorded their speakers.
Getting back to the subject for this opposition day, I will not comment on the statement by my good friend and medical colleague, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halli-day), because I have a great deal of respect for him. With regard to some of the remarks he made tonight all I will say is that I thought he knew better.
The subject of this opposition day is criticism. Why not? There is criticism all around us these days. It is an era of criticism. Everybody criticizes everybody for everything. In this particular case there is criticism with regard to federal government funding of the Medical Research Council, that it has not been sufficient to meet the growing demand of the medical science community. Often there are demands from people in an ivory tower who think that because they are in splendid isolation they are entitled to the taxpayer's dollar without supervision. In fact since 1973 the real value of government allocations to the MRC has declined in terms of 1966 constant dollars. Why not? Many other things have too, the stock market, for example.
This trend had been exacerbated further by the freeze announced on December 18, 1975, keeping this year's contribution at the same level as last year, $48.8 million. Therefore the MRC budget for 1976 is identical in real terms to that of 1969. Even with the additional $2 million provided as of May 18, 1976, it is still felt that another $4.6 million is needed for the council to meet this objective for this year. That is fair enough coming from the medical research community, and I think we all accept that.
Let us look at the reasons behind that. Federal funding has fluctuated so strongly over the past several years that it is impossible for MRC to establish a long-term strategy in the provision of research grants. That is a fair criticism and worth examining. On the other hand, however, many other things have the same difficulty in these times of inflation and recession.
A word about the nature of medical research in Canada. Unlike most other advanced western nations, notably the U.S., Britain, and France, Canada does not have any medical equivalent of a central research organization which has its own research facilities. Unlike many countries, as well, such as the U.S. and Switzerland, Canadian industry does not engage in as comprehensive medical and pharmaceutical research. Therefore most medical research here is carried out in the universities, and these are highly dependent upon outside funding, particularly from the government. It is the responsibility of the MRC then to ensure that the government subsidies are distributed to gain the maximum yield in furthering medical knowledge. That is a sacred trust to the public. As such it is purely an administrative structure.
With respect to the attitude of the scientific community toward the MRC, the medical research community is unanimous in its approval of the purpose and function of the MRC. It is also largely content with the manner in which the MRC has distributed the funds it is given. The main area of complaint remains the amount provided to the MRC for distribution.

With respect to the attitude of the medical research community toward government restraint, medical researchers are sympathetic toward the government's desire to bring the economy under control, as are all Canadians. They feel, however, that much less than being contributors to economic disorder they are victims of inflation. They feel that medical research should receive the same increases that government departments and government-conducted research facilities received last year, which averaged 16 per cent, as opposed to the MRC's budget increase of 2.9 per cent.
With regard to the funding of medical research in Canada, I wish to deal with the breakdown and perspective. From 1959 to 1963, under the Tories, federal funds provided to MRC went from $2,008,000 to $4,300,000. By 1967, under the Liberals, this figure had reached $12.3 million. From 1967 to 1976-77 federal support has more than quadrupled to $50,848,000. Over the long run, therefore, the Liberal government has demonstrated clearly its support of medical research. I emphasize over the long run.
What about the United States?

We will get to that. You like to compare us to the United States when it is in your favour, but when it does not make your point you are pretty quiet about it.
It must be kept in mind, as well, that government support of medical research does not stop with the MRC. For 1976-77 the MRC allocation of $50 million comprises only 79 per cent of all federal government support of medical research in Canada and only about 50 per cent of the over-all amount spent in this area.
For example, the MRC contributed $50,848,000, and all other government department programs $12,804,000, with a total federal expenditure for 1976-77 of $63,652,000.
The other main sources of funds for 1976-77 are contributions from provincial agencies, $12,600,000; contributions from major voluntary agencies, $19,997,000; contributions from other voluntary agencies and foundations, mainly foreign, $1,500,000. Over-all, these contributions add up to a total of $100,749,000 to be spend on medical research in Canada for this fiscal year; not bad for a small, young country.
I wish to say a word about participation of the voluntary sector. Over the past ten years contributions from the voluntary sector have kept pace with the growth of the MRC budget, quadrupling from $5 million to about $20 million. This growth in participation has been attributed to gradual improvement in the medical research community's ability to publicize its cause, as well as better organization in efforts of the contributing organizations themselves. Aid from the voluntary sector is quite uneven, however, with some groups increasing their contributions substantially, others remaining constant, and yet others decreasing their financial support.
With respect to private industry, apparently the MRC has never made direct representations for support of medical research. Personally I think that is unfortunate. I have had experience, as perhaps other members have, in this area. It is an area which is very important in many other countries. I mentioned before, the United States and Switzerland. It is an area where Canada has not even begun to
June 15, 1976

scratch the surface. There is a great deal of potential there in spite of the fact that most of our private industry is foreign owned and controlled. A lot of people think that is perhaps an inhibiting factor to the private sector. I believe a great deal more can be done.
I also wish to say a word about government explanation of medical research funding cutbacks. The government is aware that many worth-while projects have suffered as a result of its cutbacks in this field, but it is felt that no area of government spending can be fully exempted from the government's current austerity program designed to overcome the most pressing immediate problem, namely, inflation. It is wrong to look only at the last two or three years and assume this represents a typical pattern in the government's attitude toward medical research. Combating inflation, hopefully, will not be a permanent preoccupation for the government. I think if we honestly look we will see some significant early results in the battle against inflation, in fact in all of the industrialized countries in the western part of world, as recently reported by the OECD.
It is acknowledged by the government that contributions to medical research are inadequate at the present time. Certainly they are more inadequate than we would like them to be. But this inadequate funding is seen as such only in contrast to a previous decade of reasonably generous support. Regarding the need for stability in funding from one year to the next, this too is acknowledged by the minister to be a serious problem. What is lacking is a workable formula or set of criteria whereby an appropriate growth rate can be determined for funding. The minister for science referred to that today and I believe the matter is being seriously considered.
There are a number of arguments which might be put forward in defence of the current level of government funding of research. For example, how is one to determine what is the optimum level of federal funding? This is a problem in all areas of federal funding. There is no easy answer. It has to be arbitrary. Is all research good? Is all research valuable and worth while, particularly when it is done with the taxpayers' money? Hopefully the situation will change, but in this area there is resistance, there is unfamiliarity with business management, with cost accounting, with the setting of strict objectives, particularly in the basic research area, and our changing times demand a more cost-efficient approach.
Even if certain research is deemed imperative, must it be expensive? Yes, a great deal of it must be expensive, but must it all be expensive, or as expensive as it is? After all, the greatest medical discovery, that for which this country is famous around the world, was the discovery of insulin, and this was done on an extremely low budget, using very simple means.
The opposition talks at times about return on investment. The official opposition critic referred to a number of discoveries in respect to which there has been good return on the money spent. That is true in those cases. But the information he gave us is a bit loaded. He was speaking only about the research which has worked; the examples given did not reflect the cost of all the research which is carried out.
Medical Research
The government must weigh demands from many different sectors in society. Every one of them has a legitimate claim for more funds. As we all say these days, everybody wants decreased government spending but nobody wants particular cuts. Where would the critics have us make these cuts, in transport? In a country like this? In regional expansion? In social welfare? In development of culture, in communications-
We showed you where you could save a billion.

-in native and northern development, in health and sports? In business and economics, where a great deal of money goes? In foreign aid, perhaps? Would they have us make cuts there? It is easy to say these things when you are not in government, when you are the critics. Particularly during times such as these, when the government must lead efforts in restraint to bring the economy back in line, the administration can expect to be subject to particularly strong pressure from all sectors attempting to avoid the squeeze. This kind of austerity should provide needed pressure on the researchers themselves to encourage maximum efficiency and rationalization in their operations. There is no question about that.
In prosperous times everyone grows a bit fat-the universities are no exception and the research laboratories are no exception either. The university organizations themselves have been concerned about this. They have set up studies to encourage rationalization, to increase efficiency, to prevent duplication. In industry when we were approached for funds, when we were approached to buy expensive equipment for university departments, we often found that the equipment requested was already there in another department, next door. It was simply duplication. Yet the two researchers had not talked to each other about it, had not co-ordinated their requests. This would have been money down the drain had somebody not been careful.
Times such as this should as well provide an added opportunity for researchers and private industry to get together to their mutual benefit. The greatest potential for increasing funds for medical research lies in one heretofore untapped reserve-and I referred to this a little earlier, Mr. Speaker-a process of working together involving private industry, government, and universities. It is well done in many countries, by countries such as our great neighbour, the United States, by many European countries, particularly Switzerland. There seems to be some disinclination in this country for these sectors to work together. In the meantime the work is not getting done or, if it is getting done, it is being achieved in a more expensive way.
I would like to quote from a committee report of May 18, 1976, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare was addressing the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. He said:
I am advised by Dr. Bois that the MRC itself has not made representations to private industry about contributions to medical research.
That would be my impression as well. I think the situation is the same with the universities and private industry-a certain aloofness which is a little hard to define and hard to explain.

June 15, 1976
Medical Research
As I said before, various members of this House have had some direct experience with medical research, some of us in private industry, and we found that in great contrast to other countries the co-ordinated effort simply is not there. Private industry does possess considerable resources and it is my experience that if the effort were shown on both sides, foreignowned or not, they would be more than willing to work with our research community and help answer a great deal of our concern about funding. At one time, when with industry, I recall approaching the head of MRC, a very fine man who has done a fine job in most of his functions, with a concrete offer for some kind of tripartite arrangement between MRC, the universities, and industry, to work together for a better research effort than we could do alone. Mr. Speaker, there was no significant response. Yet MRC has performed most of its functions well. But both the MRC and the universities will have to look at their relations with areas such as private industry to generate new funds and to use the funds they have more efficiently.
I also believe that medical research in this country has a great friend in the deputy minister for science, Maurice LeClair, with whom I have discussed this subject. He certainly knows medical research and is very sympathetic to the cause, including this concern about funding. I believe, by the same-

Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Has the hon. member the consent of the House to continue?
Agreed.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I will wrap up my remarks very briefly. I believe time will prove that medical research in this country has a very great friend in the Minister of National Health and Welfare, indeed in members on the entire government side. I believe that all members of parliament and the general public too are appreciative of the research community. But there are problems which must be worked out. There is no sense kidding ourselves. One of our concerns must be the efficiency with which funds are used, and whether we are experiencing difficult economic times or normal ones, those things must be worked out. If we do this we will be a better research country and a better medical community for having done so.
In the meantime I think it is fair to say that our researchers will need to come down from their ivory towers and learn a little more about what the world in general is like. They will need to learn to sell to the public and to the government their very important function better than has been the case in the past, and thus compete with all the other important and vital needs that are facing this country. I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and would like to thank other hon. members of the House for giving me the extra time.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to listen to the remarks on

this subject of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) who said that he had had experience in the field of medical research. Be that as it may, I would say from the tone of his remarks that he also indicated he had had very little experience in the field of economics.
This debate on the failure of the government to give adequate priority to health research funding in Canada takes place in an interesting context. A first ministers' conference has just concluded at which a major item on the agenda was a revision of the cost sharing arrangements with the provinces for the medical care and hospital insurance programs. Including the value of abated tax points to the province of Quebec, these programs will, according to the estimates, cost the federal treasury approximately $4 billion this fiscal year. One of the goals sought by the federal government at the first ministers' conference was to hold down the rate of growth of these expenditures through the implementation of a new formula.
The sum of $4 billion is an impressive amount of money in anyone's language. One of the aspects of this debate revolves around a smaller and less impressive amount, the approximately $4 million in additional funding that is required to maintain the level of medical research at last year's standard. The bearing that these two amounts have on one another is very important.
I want to say at the outset that I am fed up with the stock response we always hear from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), which has just been reiterated by the hon. member for Halton, when the request is made for additional funding for medical research by members from this side of the House. We have all heard that response, Mr. Speaker: It goes something like this, "You are always telling us to restrain government spending. We practice it in this specific area and now you complain. Why can't you be consistent?"
That is a phony argument, and the hon. minister, who I regret is not here tonight, shows his contempt for the House by employing it. If he does not know that it is a phony argument then he does not know the difference between restraint and false economy, between being penny wise and pound foolish.
The whole point of our argument, which the President of the Treasury Board has never refuted or even attempted to refute, is that this is an expenditure that will not only save lives-a consideration that I would hope would be of some importance to him-but it is an investment that will save the federal and the provincial taxpayer money that will more than repay that investment.
The so-called restraint that has been imposed on Medical Research Council funding, following a cutback in funding, is equivalent to a cost cutting program in a business that begins by terminating the fire insurance policy or deferring replacement of worn out machinery that must be kept in operation to keep unit costs down.
The savings the minister boasts of today are in reality ensuring higher costs in the future, and probably in the very near future. If the aim is to hold down health care costs, let us not throw away the tools that will enable us to do so not just this year, but on a long term basis, perhaps in some cases even on a permanent basis. An ounce of prevention is still worth a pound of cure. Four million
June 15, 1976

dollars more this year may save us tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars later on; and if that seems extreme, consider how much it would cost us today in treatment, rehabilitation, and welfare to care for those potential victims of polio who were saved from that dread disease by the discovery of Salk vaccine.
Many Canadians, both members of this House and countless thousands across the country, have pleaded the case for increased medical research funding on humanitarian grounds and on the hope for a better quality of life. I think of the many people who have written to me expressing their concern at the government's insensitivity to the need for more research funds. I think not only of medical researchers-although many of them have written me-but of concerned citizens who consider the good health of Canadians to be one of the nation's prime assets. Many were prompted to write because of personal knowledge of the ravages of as yet unconquered diseases. Some have family, friends or relatives who stand to benefit from breakthroughs in the major diseases threatening mankind today-cancer, heart disease, multiple sclerosis, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis. Many others simply expressed their understanding of the need to use our financial resources wisely in researching new methods to combat disease.
Canadians are interested, tremendously interested, in this matter. Each year through voluntary donations they give a large amount of money to medical research. And their interest is such that each year their contributions increase, up 20 per cent this year over last year. Ordinary Canadians are doing their part, but at the same time they have had to watch the government reducing its commitment in this field.
For every dollar spent in research today there is a saving of $20 in 10 years' time-some estimates of the cost-benefit ratio are even higher. This represents a better than 20 to 1 payoff on investment-an opportunity that no businessman could resist-but an investment that the government fails to comprehend. Dr. Vivian Abrahams, a medical researcher and teacher at Queen's University, one of these researchers who the member of parliament for Halton says continually live in an ivory tower, in his appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) summed up the frustation of so many researchers when he said:
This generation has benefited hugely by the efforts of previous generations and we have a responsibility to generations to come to devote a reasonable and fair proportion of our resources to the support of medical research.
The direct savings in future medical care costs are convincing enough, Mr. Speaker, but equally important is the potential contribution to the Gross National Product through earnings and productivity of the many who have been spared, because of the successes of our medical research teams, the crippling effects of once terrifying diseases and even premature death.
The economic logic for increased support of medical research is so compelling that it is the ultimate in frustration and bewilderment to witness the lethargy of the government over the past few years in allowing the erosion of the medical health research capability of this country, with all the demoralizing consequences that that entails. What is happening in the field of medical research is indicative
Medical Research
of the government's negative approach to science and technology, as was so well set out by my colleague from Halton-Wentworth during a recent debate in this House on science policy.
What the government does not seem to realize and does not seem to comprehend is that the prime requisite in successful scientific research is continuity. It cannot be turned off and on like a tap, and yet that is the course the government has been following.
In the middle and late 1960's the government moved to alleviate the inadequacies of the facilities in our medical schools and research labs. This period was marked by considerable expansion in Canada's medical schools, with a clear understanding of the symbiotic relationship of research and teaching to an over-all improvement in the quality of our medical schools. Ten years later, just as Canada is moving into a position to enjoy the fruits of this investigation, we are witnessing instead the painful and slow dissolution of our research capacity caused by government restraint in medical research funding.
We cannot afford to lose our bright young medical researchers. We cannot afford it in economic terms, and we cannot afford it in human terms. But, because of uncertainty and declining opportunities in the field of medical research, there has been a serious reduction in the number of medical graduates entering the research field. Only 1 per cent of graduates is expected to go into research this year as compared to 5 per cent in 1970.
Dr. Alex Sehon, head of the Department of Immunology of the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Manitoba said recently:
It is absolutely essential to the success of our biomedical research that we provide for our brightest young people the appropriate milieu to develop their talents. These are among the best dollars we can spend in terms of the value received. Clearly, no investment in research can be expected to yield its full harvest by an "on-again and off-again" policy which puts the whole research establishment in a state of chaos and does not allow for long-term planning. Neither parliament nor the Canadian public can expect to reap the promising harvest of medical research by discouraging potential research workers from entering a research career, when the continuance of research activities by existing medical scientists is being threatened.
And threatened that future is in Canada, threatened by the government. Studies and statistics can be cited to prove it.
A study in process by the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges shows that there has been a decline of 23 per cent in the past four years in the number of medical research grants per 100 students in our medical schools. Figures for this year show that 127 projects which the Medical Research Council's selection committee considered of sufficient calibre to be worthy of funding had to be turned down because of the lack of funding; because of the lack of $4.6 million. If you want to put that figure in another way, that is 3/20ths of 1 per cent of the over-all health care budget of the federal government. That is 3/20ths of 1 per cent of what the government now spends trying to correct the health state of this country. As I mentioned earlier, this is a government that is penny wise and pound foolish.
