Medical Research
Harry Gunning, President of the University of Alberta, summed it up well in a speech last month to graduating classes of the university when he said:
There are obviously many ways in which the federal government can push this nation towards bankruptcy. Perhaps the most efficient method of achieving this undesirable goal is to so stifle and starve the innovative spirit of this country that we are forced to rely almost entirely on other countries to provide us with the highly sophisticated goods and services that we must develop as an industrialized scientific nation. In this respect the present government is doing an outstanding job.
Canada is a highly industrialized nation. Our researchers are held in high regard throughout the world. Yet the erosion of our medical research capability will transform us into medical mendicants when it is incumbent on us to be developing excellence in this field here in Canada to alleviate the problems of less developed nations. Is Canada to be a parasite on the developed nations, importing medical advances from other developed countries? Where is our sense of pride? What has happened to our ambition to want to contribute rather than borrow? This government recognizes neither.
A growing concern in the scientific community, and one which deserves immediate attention, is the thrust of the government's science policy to encourage targeted or mission-oriented research at the expense of basic research. The resulting imbalance in the various research divisions has serious implications for our scientific effort.
Applications for targeted research quickly become known throughout the scientific community as "safe", that is, more likely to be successful in receiving funds from the Medical Research Council. Applicants understandably are tempted to tailor their proposals to strengthen their chances of obtaining grants. If the tendency on the part of the government to recognize targeted research continues, basic research will suffer. Testimony after testimony from scientific researchers supports the necessity of giving priority to basic research.
I should like to quote from an article by Dr. Louis Siminivitch, geneticist-in-chief, Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto. He says:
The idea that scientists are self-serving and are not directing their efforts to the important problems of our society also represents a lack of understanding of the scientific process. Practical problems such as the development of treatment modalities for disease or the solution of energy problems, are also not solved in a vacuum. Their investigation also rests on the total body of knowledge in science and, in fact, many such problems may simply not be resolvable at this time because of the absence of key fundamental facts. The development of a vaccine for polio or of the laser required knowledge gleaned from several directions by many investigators of various levels of quality, and over many years. The importance of the polio vaccine and the utility of laser in problems as diverse as subway construction and eye surgery, need not be elaborated here. What is important is to realize that these are not isolated examples, and they are introduced here just to underline the fact that the development of medical cures and other such practical advances are, of necessity, a continuous process which feeds on what many might consider to be basic non-practical research. The lack of recognition and support of a strong basic science effort mortgages our ability as a nation to meet the many important practical challenges of the future.
Dr. Fudenberg of the Faculty of Medicine of the University of California said, and this is interesting to note:
Had funds been awarded for "practical research" in the late 1940's, they would have been to build a better respirator-and perhaps polio would not still be with us.

In fact a comprehensive study by Comroe and Dripps shows conclusively that of the major advances in certain areas of medicine, basic research had yielded key discoveries almost twice as often as all other types of research and development, yet the government's tendency is to downgrade basic research.
I began my remarks by making reference to efforts to restrain health care costs at the first minister's conference during the past two days. Let me conclude by referring to another recent development in federal-provincial relations designed, I presume, to serve the same purpose. I refer to the health review and the proposals made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to the provincial health ministers earlier this spring to share the cost of relatively inexpensive alternative services to hospital and medical care in return for a commitment to hold down costs in those relatively expensive areas. This proposal has much to commend it, but surely only a minister with tunnel vision would fail to see that a review designed to shift the focus from high to low-cost health services in the interests of restraint must include as an integral element an adequately funded medical research program designed to seek more efficient and effective alternatives to present treatment methods. Some money will be saved by treating people out of hospitals once they fall ill. Considerably more money will be saved if you invest in research that may prevent illness in the first place or shorten the period of time in treatment facilities.
Those solutions will come not only from targeted research in specific areas but as spin-offs from pure research and from research in related fields. But we must give those discoveries a chance to happen with adequate research funding, and not delude ourselves into thinking we save money by short-changing those research scientists who will hold down our costs in the future. Even disregarding the economics of this expenditure, the case for it in terms of human lives, human health, and maintaining a cadre of trained research personnel in this country is overwhelming.

Mr. Speaker, the topic before us today, that of an appropriate level of funding by the federal government for medical research, is an important one with serious implications for the lives of Canadians.
As was pointed out in the preface to "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians," a working document published by the Department of National Health and Welfare in 1974:
Good health is the bedrock on which social progress is built. A nation of healthy people can do those things that make life worth while, and as the level of health increases so does the potential for happiness.
The fundamental importance of measures to maintain and improve good physical and mental health has long been recognized by the provincial governments and the Government of Canada and, as a result, we have prepaid medical and hospital insurance, public health protection, programs to counter environmental pollution, accident prevention programs, and safeguards and requirements for food and drugs. Medical research, whether in-house research carried out directly by the Department of National Health and Welfare, or research funded by the department through the Medical Research Council, or research funded by private organizations cannot be considered in a vacuum but must be seen as one factor in a very broad spectrum of factors that contribute to the health, happiness, and quality of life of Canadians.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), in his preface to "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", commenting on the fact that physicians, surgeons, nurses, and hospitals spend much of their time treating ills caused by environmental factors and behavioural risks, stated:
It is evident now that further improvements in the environment and reductions in self-imposed risks .. . are necessary if more Canadians are to live a full, happy, long and illness-free life.
At a national symposium on health research priorities held at McGill University on May 25, 1973, the point was made that many proven advances resulting from basic and clinical research are not being applied at the level of the practising physician. If one accepts this, one might see measures for more co-ordinated and effective use of existing knowledge as having higher priority than the search for new knowledge.
Examination of mortality figures in Canada shows a very high proportion of deaths which with our present
Medical Research
knowledge could be avoided. For example, the highest single cause of death in males between 15 and 24 is the motor vehicle accident. Other accidents, whether domestic accidents in the case of young children or industrial accidents, also account for a disconcertingly high proportion of deaths. Avoidable diseases of life style including those relating to abuse of tobacco, alcohol, or drugs take a high toll.
Another concern that emerged from the McGill symposium was that an insufficient proportion of research money is allocated to clinical, socio-medical, and organizational aspects of health and health care. This is not an issue of which we have heard much in recent months. The groups who have been lobbying members of parliament have placed their emphasis, for the most part, on basic biological research. Many of the people we have seen, too, have been unwilling to come to terms with the important questions of priorities and with choosing among conflicting options. One scientist, whom I asked for an indication of his priorities, told me that all applications from universities should be funded, that there is no possibility of bad or incompetent research being done in universities because of the peer review system.
You should quote his name.

I find this somewhat less than realistic. No group in society can claim an unlimited right to have their productions unexplained, unexamined by members of other disciplines, and funded uncritically with tax dollars.
At the other end of the scale from the person who says all applications for medical research from universities should be funded, is the person who is extremely critical of all work that is not done in his or her own department. The working paper "A New Perspective" commented on the need for researchers to develop:
.. . a unity of purpose which has often been lacking because of the destructive competition for limited funds. Balanced progress in all fields can only be obtained when researchers pull together toward the common objective of raising the health status of Canadians.
A very gentlemanly sidestepping of anything that looked like "destructive competition" was achieved by a member of a group lobbying for "more research" who, when I asked him to define areas which he considered priorities, explained that his organization represented people with many interests and could not promote any one area of endeavour without offending some members.
The Oliver Twist cry for "more" is understandable but is singularly unhelpful to legislators unless it is defined and some priorities set in terms of contemporary health needs.
Prior to 1974 the federal government limited its activities in the health field to its traditional responsibilities such as quarantine medicine, protection of the food supply, product safety, ensuring accessibility to personal health care through financial assistance to provincial health insurance plans, and financing research. The basis for concentrating its interest in these areas was the belief that the improvement of personal health care was the principal means of raising the level of health of Canadians.
The 1974 working paper, "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", stated:

The evidence uncovered by the analysis of underlying causes of sickness and death now indicates that improvement in the environment and an abatement in the level of risks imposed upon themselves by individuals, taken together, constitute the most promising ways by which further advances can be made.
The paper continues:
Accordingly, it is the intention of the government of Canada, first, to maintain at a high level the services and support provided through its present activities in health protection, research and the financing of personal health care. To these will be added measures directed at specific national health problems, chosen in consultation with provinces, consumers, professions and associations according to their gravity and incidence, and aimed at removing or reducing the factors underlying sickness and death.
Some of these measures in time will no doubt be directed at environmental factors; others will be directed at lifestyle risks; still others will expand the horizons of health research and yet others will encourage more personal care services to neglected parts of the Canadian population ...
Since direct health care is already consuming some 7 per cent of the wealth that Canadians produce annually, it is evident that the rate at which the Government of Canada can expand its activities in the field of health is severely limited by financial considerations. It is also true that measures directed at the prevention of illness will take some time before they are translated into savings in the costs of providing curative health services.
Later the report went on to say:
... with the recognition that the good health of Canadians is an objective that shines brightly above .. . special interest groups, the Government of Canada proposes to take steps that will start the nation on the road to levels of health even higher than those that Canada now enjoys.
To achieve the aims of reducing mental and physical health hazards for Canadians whose risks are high and improving access to good health care, five strategies were proposed:
(1)	A health promotion strategy aimed at informing, influencing, and assisting both individuals and organizations so that they will accept more responsibility and be more active in matters affecting mental and physical health.
(2)	A regulatory strategy aimed at using federal regulatory powers to reduce hazards to mental and physical health, and at encouraging and assisting provinces to use their regulatory powers to the same end.
(3)	A research Strategy designed to help discover and apply knowledge needed to solve mental and physical health problems.
(4)	A health care efficiency strategy the objective of which shall be to help the provinces reorganize the system for delivering mental and physical health care so that the three elements of cost, accessibility and effectiveness are balanced in the interest of Canadians.
(5)	A goal-setting strategy the purpose of which will be to set, in co-operation with others, goals for raising the level of the mental and physical health of Canadians and improving the efficiency of the health care system.
The paper contains 74 proposals of which 15 deal with research. These are:
1.	An ongoing dialogue between health planners and the research community on the priorities for mission-oriented health research while preserving for the research community the setting of priorities in basic research.
2.	The implementation of a regular national health survey to determine the prevalence and nature of acute and chronic mental and physical illness, to permit an assessment of the health status and needs of Canadians and to measure changes in status and needs.
3.	The institution of a special program for identifying health status indicators and high-risk segments of the Canadian population, for the evaluation of the nature and gravity of mental and physical health risks, and for the proposal of measures to abate the level of risk.

4.	Measures to help integrate, improve and use, on a national basis, the data and statistics being recorded at various governmental and institutional levels.
5.	The establishment of a well-designed comprehensive system for the reporting of accident statistics which would, among other things, identify accident-associated products.
6.	The promotion of increased support for research on underlying causes of coronary-artery disease.
7.	Support for more research on the cause and treatment of mental illness.
8.	The support of projects designed to evaluate the results of present mass-screening programs and to test the effectiveness of future ones.
9.	The establishment of a national drug abuse institute covering all abusive drugs including psychotropic drugs, both licit and illicit, alcohol and cigarettes, and responsible for gathering statistics, supporting research, evaluating preventive and treatment measures and recommending policy.
10.	The undertaking of a broad continuing study into the ways and means of effectively informing the Canadian people on changes in behaviour which will significantly reduce self-imposed risks.
11.	The continuation and strengthening of present research into the effect of the physical environment on health.
12.	The establishment of a program for assessing the effect of social and environmental change on health, including the calculation of risk factors due to lifestyle.
13.	The continuation of support for research on physical and mental fitness and for fitness testing.
14.	Continued and increased support for research into better ways of providing health care.
15.	Continued support for research consistent with the scale of the health care industry.
The emphasis on applied or clinical research as opposed to basic research is clear: but obviously the position of the latter is protected, especially by recommendations Nos. I and 15.
Within the Department of National Health and Welfare a sum of $11,088,000 has been assigned this year to the national health research and development program. Some of the representations received in recent months from university employed scientists have expressed opposition to in-house research but have not offered reasons for their opposition and, in the absence of clearly stated reasons and supporting data, I cannot accept that research, in order to be valid, must be completely controlled by a university.
Several provinces have allocated moneys to health research or have indicated that they intend to do so. The voluntary sector is increasingly supporting research.
Finally, let me turn to the Medical Research Council for which main estimates for 1976-77 provide $48,848,000 for research support programs, and $1,142,000 for administrative costs. To put these votes in perspective it may be useful to remember that for 1966-67, a decade ago, main estimates provided $12.3 million for research support through the Medical Research Council. This figure has therefore almost quadrupled in the intervening ten years. The present provision of $48.8 million represents 79 per cent of the support for research provided this year by federal agencies, including the Department of National Health and Welfare, which have some major responsibility for health research. It is about 49 per cent of the total support expected to reach extramural health research in Canada this year from all sources.
On December 18, 1975, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) reported to the House a decision to limit the actual increase for the Medical Research Council
June 15, 1976

over 1975-76 to $1,414,000. Subsequent to that decision the Minister of National Health and Welfare stated that he had been able to re-allocate an additional $2 million from within his department to the Medical Research Council. This limiting of the rate of growth has been misrepresented as a cut in the funds available for medical research.
It may very well be that more funds should be allocated for medical research this year, but the onus is on those who think so to make the case more clearly and effectively than they have done to date, and to state unequivocally what elements of health programs should be given up or reduced in order to free additional funds.

Stop being political. Open your ears. Talk to the medical and health leaders of this country. They will tell you that because of the shortsightedness of the government, services at the local level are slowly but surely slipping from excellence to mediocrity.

Oh, oh!

Mr. Minister, if you do not have anything better to do, go out and amuse yourself. Don't intervene in this debate. You are doing a bad enough job running your own portfolio.
I have already said, and I believe the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) alluded to this, we are not just talking about pure biomedical research, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) talked about. We are talking about clinical research, research in education, basic research in terms of how better can we, not in an institutional way, deliver medical and health care services. There is no use talking about savings in medicare or medical and health care programs until we put some meaningful research dollars into the whole area of how we are better going to deliver medical health care services.
An hon. member alluded in a political way to what the premier of Ontario is doing. He knows what the premier of Ontario is doing. He is finally doing what the former Minister of National Health and Welfare said years ago. We must have meaningful planning where the community hospital is the central institution for the total delivery of medical and health care services. The minute one premier has the guts and do on the local level what the federal government should have been doing in the past four or five years, what do you say? Politics. The Ontario minister of health has been a statesman in many instances.

subtopic: AIR CANADA-DISPUTE WITH EMPLOYEES OF FINANCE BRANCH IN WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE
AIR CANADA-DISPUTE WITH EMPLOYEES OF FINANCE BRANCH IN WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past few weeks I have been calling for a complete examination of the Air Canada finance department operation in Winnipeg by the Auditor General's department because of the huge deficit experienced by Air Canada in 1975 amounting to $12.5 million; and for the first four months of 1976 the deficit has reached $14.5 million.
Before listing further reasons for the necessity for a complete examination into Air Canada's affairs, it is my understanding that a new Air Canada act is to be introduced by the government later this year which would separate Air Canada from being audited by an auditor appointed by the CNR, which makes a lot of sense. But due to the gravity of the situation in Winnipeg, the government is obligated to take immediate action to clean up the mess.
The government's repeated answer to me that MP's can question Air Canada in committee is nothing but a cover up. The committee system is not the area to conduct an audit; nor are MP's able to conduct an audit and investigate whether Air Canada has proper accounting procedures. Air Canada should appear before the committee for questioning in other areas.
A proper audit can only be done by qualified accountants and auditors who would have to spend considerable time at the finance branch examining Air Canada's procedures. Further, Mr. Speaker, the auditor's report contained in the 1975 Air Canada report from Cooper and Lybrand of Ottawa states that their examination includes a general review of the accounting procedures. It would seem that their terms of reference must be very limited.
Serious charges of financial mismanagement have been laid by CALEA and they have been documented charges, not supposition. An Air Canada public relations officer has denied these charges and has stated that the air line is subject to continuous external audit procedures by independent auditors appointed by the federal government. "We are under constant scrutiny", he said.
I have discussed this matter with Air Canada employees and they inform me that no independent auditors have scrutinized their procedures at all. So, Mr. Speaker, we have a direct contradiction and a further reason for an immediate investigation to be conducted into Air Canada's financial procedures, which were highly criticized in the Estey report.

Also, Mr. Speaker, a member of the accounting firm of Touche, Ross and Company has stated that if Air Canada had realistic accounting procedures the 1975 loss would be about $100 million instead of the reported $12.5 million. This is a serious charge and cannot just be swept under the rug.
Further charges have been laid by CALEA that the present billing work being contracted out across Canada is a cover-up designed to "get rid of all the embarrassing material". To date the contracting out of Air Canada finance work has cost a quarter of a million dollars. This ridiculous practice should be stopped and all billing work returned to the finance branch in Winnipeg. I am informed the contracted work is returned with a 50 per cent error factor, further compounding the problem.
The Saturday, June 12 edition of the Winnipeg Free Press in a front page copyrighted article by John Sullivan under the headline "Work Slowdown, Mismanagement Cost Air Canada Millions" stated:
Millions of dollars in revenue has been lost or written off by Air Canada in the last year because of inadequate or non-existent auditing practices, according to confidential financial reports by the airline's strike-bound Winnipeg financial workers.
In releasing the reports to the Free Press this week, local officials of the Canadian Airline Employees' Association . . . said a lack of adequate financial control has cost the publicly-owned airline enough revenue to "almost or perhaps totally" account for Air Canada's record $12.4 million deficit last year.
The financial study, conducted by union leaders late last year, says Air Canada has written off millions of dollars in unreported ticket sales by airline sales offices, travel agents and commercial subscribers.
I should like to remind the parliamentary secretary, who I assume is here to answer me tonight, that we are dealing with a Crown corporation and the taxpayers' money. This is not a private organization and we cannot have repeated slough-offs like I have been receiving over the past few weeks. The article continues;
More millions have been lost because the airline is simply paying out refunds and flight coupon billings from other airlines and accepting sales reports from travel agents and commercial subscribers without auditing them for errors, the union claims.
Interest on this revenue which has been lost, as well as the Crown airline's practice of farming out financial work to private firms in recent months, because of a huge backlog in processing, has also cost millions, the study says.
In short, the union leaders say Air Canada financial controls are in a mess, aggravated but not caused by the long-simmering labour dispute:
"The problem is one where the system originally devised for the audit and accounting process of the finance branch cannot accommodate the volume of work. Until such time as an automated process relieves the congestion, or until an adequate level of trained staff is reached, Air Canada will continue to have no protection for its revenues-strike or no strike".
I have also pointed this out to the parliamentary secretary and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on a number of occasions. The article then states:
The CALEA study apparently was written and released to the union's membership last year in a series of "progress reports" on the effects of a work slowdown and work-to-rule campaign by the employees.
Contract negotiations between Air Canada and the union-which began last April-broke down in December over the issues of job security and employee classifications-



June 15, 1976

This has nothing to do with poor accounting procedures. -after the existing contract expired August 25. The dispute is now under federal mediation but CALEA's slowdown and rotating strikes have continued for months with no end in sight.
The union says an Air Canada official at corporate headquarters in Montreal had admitted to them last year that "labour unrest in the accounting services division was costing $300,000 a week and this has been going on for two years."
A high-ranking official at the Winnipeg finance branch-

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR CANADA-DISPUTE WITH EMPLOYEES OF FINANCE BRANCH IN WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO SETTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation in Winnipeg, as my hon. friend knows, is a particularly difficult one because of the various circumstances he has described this evening and on other occasions in the House. We have two separate issues involved that continue to complicate one another, and continue to muddle the situation. On the one hand we have a very difficult and complex labour situation, and on the other we have the allegations that have been made about faulty accounting and auditing procedures in that particular part of Air Canada's finance branch.
The labour situation described by the hon. member has, indeed, been under discussion for a very long period of time. Relatively recently, of course, we have had the submission of the report of the conciliation commissioner which has been reviewed by the company, the union, and the Department of Labour in light of the anti-inflation program.
The issue which has kept the two parties apart the longest in connection with the labour dispute, as the hon. member knows, is the matter of job descriptions and job security. For the past two years Air Canada has devoted an enormous amount of time, money, and effort in an attempt to resolve this issue. The advice of two outside consulting authorities has been sought, and when their various proposals did not prove acceptable to the union a commissioner, Mr. D. J. Jessiman, was named by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). Negotiations which had broken off in the early spring of 1975 were resumed under his jurisdiction in July last year. They continued until mid-September when the union requested the commissioner to take evidence and submit his report.
As I say, every effort has been made by the government and the company to bring this lengthy dispute to a conclusion. At the same time as the discussion on the labour dispute has been going on, we have had as well the problem that has been mentioned by my hon. friend in connection with the auditing matters.
As he has mentioned this evening we do have before parliament and the country the very comprehensive Estey Report into this whole question affecting Air Canada which, as he mentioned again tonight, will result in useful legislation. There is, as he has mentioned as well, an outside auditing procedure already in place, and there are also the ultimate safeguards of parliamentary scrutiny of the operations of Crown corporations. Beyond those assurances and the explanation with respect to the complicating factors of the labour dispute interfering with the other matter, I think for the time being this evening that is where I would leave the explanation.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED BREAK-IN OF QUEBEC NEWSPAPER OFFICE BY MEMBERS OF THE FORCE
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED BREAK-IN OF QUEBEC NEWSPAPER OFFICE BY MEMBERS OF THE FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure there are many members in this House of Commons who, like myself, would like some more background on the rather bizarre sounding incident of our national police force, the RCMP, breaking into the premises of a Quebec newspaper sometime ago. I know that members of all parties have asked questions about it. I recall the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) asking a question about it on behalf of the Social Credit Party. My friend the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) also made an inquiry in this House about the information and background surrounding this incident.
Tonight, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to make another appeal to the minister or his parliamentary secretary to give the House of Commons a little information. The minister indicated on several occasions he would do this. If my memory does not play me false, I think it was on March 31 of this year that he indicated he hoped to give the House as much information as was possible once he received an RCMP report on the matter. On April 2 he repeated that remark in effect, and again on April 28, I believe as recorded at page 12952 of Hansard, he said the same thing for the third time. Then on May 18 he admitted that he had received a full report from the RCMP, but instead of reporting to this House as he had promised he turned the report over to the Quebec Solicitor General to, as he said, determine whether something illegal had taken place.
Any force as large and complex as the RCMP inevitably makes mistakes. They are entitled to make a few mistakes because most of the time they do a tremendous job. But like fire, the RCMP is a good servant but a bad master. If there are occasions, and we all know there are, when mistakes are made, I think it is incumbent on the minister who is responsible for the conduct of our national police force to come into the House of Commons and tell us in effect what went wrong. I do not wish to go into many incidents to make my point, but I think it is of some interest that, for instance, here in Ottawa on the very premises of parliament a member of the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires and his family were considerably embarrassed by the RCMP who made what turned out to be an unfortunate mistake by coming into his premises on a mistaken apprehension that there may have been drugs there. This of course resulted in an action being taken against them, for which this man and his family were compensated. That is fine. We all understand this.
What I would like to know, and I am sure other members would like to know, is what the implications are in respect of this unfortunate incident with regard to the Quebec newspaper L'Agence de Presse Libre du Quebec. Obviously there was no warrant. The RCMP took part in a joint venture with other police forces. I would like to know more about this. Whose responsibility was it to have made certain that the entry was done properly? Perhaps under the circumstances it could not have been done properly, which makes it all the more serious.

June 15, 1976
Adjournment Debate
Without straying too far off the subject I would like to say that so far as I am concerned I really believe that the rank and file members of the RCMP would support a crackdown, or a check, on some of the procedures and methods used on occasion which result in these unfortunate types of incidents. It would be a good idea for the responsible ministers and the government to exercise a little bit more supervision over the force. However, I will not talk on that topic because that is not the issue here tonight.
I would like to remind the parliamentary secretary that as a member of parliament I feel that this House is entitled to more information about this incident than we have received. It is all very well for the solicitor general for the province of Quebec to have an investigation to ascertain what happened. He has responsibilities there as well to see what part the force played vis-a-vis MUC or the Quebec provincial police, but there is only one minister responsible to the House of Commons for the RCMP, and that is the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand).
So without saying anything more this evening I am simply inviting the parliamentary secretary to give us as much information as he can and to assure us that this incident, which has rather alarming overtones, was in fact an isolated one and that remedial steps will be taken. Without wanting to sound as if I were asking that people be punished if mistakes were made, I want to remind the parliamentary secretary again that members of the force in the past have been severely disciplined, and often discharged without a hearing, for incidents which on the face of it sound to me a great deal less serious than permitting something like this to happen with respect to that procedure, whatever it was, affecting the rights of this small newspaper in Quebec.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED BREAK-IN OF QUEBEC NEWSPAPER OFFICE BY MEMBERS OF THE FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to be as co-operative as I can with the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). I know he has a real concern in these matters and he has made it a special interest of his in the House. He is very well aware of the fact that the Solicitor General of the province of Quebec is responsible for the administration of justice in that province and it is he who must determine the need for a complete investigation of all the facts from all the police forces involved and whether or not further charges should be laid in this matter. However, I will attempt to provide further information to the hon. member who last June 8 asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) if he was prepared to give the House a complete report on the break and entry into the L'agence de Presse Libre du Quebec.
As most hon. members are aware, this break in is supposed to have occurred in 1972. The minister did not become aware of the break in until 1976. Upon learning of it the minister requested details from the RCMP. Officials in the RCMP were able to confirm that there was a break in and that officers of the RCMP, along with members of the Montreal Urban Community Police Force and the Quebec Police Force were involved in this act. Originally the minister stated that the RCMP had played a supportive role, but later was informed that the event was a combined

effort. He was also informed that as far as the RCMP were concerned there was no warrant obtained before the break-in.
The RCMP have completed their investigation into the role which any of its officers may have played in this break-in. The minister has also had the opportunity of discussing the matter with the Solicitor General of Quebec. On any criminal act which may have taken place in Quebec, Mr. Lalonde has asked that the RCMP report be made available to him. The report is now in his hands.
The Solicitor General wishes to emphasize that only the report of the RCMP involvement was made available to him. The reports involving the other two forces were naturally given to the Quebec Solicitor General.
The Solicitor General of Quebec will therefore be responsible for determining whether or not criminal charges should be proceeded with. The minister wishes to advise this House that any action which he may take will have to await the decision of Mr. Lalonde.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR EMBARGO ON IMPORTATION OF CHEESE
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR EMBARGO ON IMPORTATION OF CHEESE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I raise deals with a subject somewhat different from those raised by my two colleagues. I want to remind the House that on May 25, 1976, the Globe and Mail published an article which indicated that an attempt was being made to re-condition rotten imported Feta cheese for the purpose of moving this product on to our domestic market as a fresh commodity.
During the question period later that same day I raised this matter, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) replied in part:
I understand there is every possibility that this cheese was inspected when it was brought into Canada, but it has been in Canada for over a year. It was when it was brought out of storage that it was found to be unfit for human consumption.
It was found to be unfit for human consumption only after a Canadian cheese manufacturer "blew the whistle" and requested that this product be inspected. The Minister of Agriculture went on to comment that "over 4,000 inspections of imported cheese were carried out last year." Granted, Mr. Speaker, 4,000 inspections seem substantial, but one has to remember that applies to 50 million pounds. That represents only one inspection on every 12,500 pounds of imported cheese. It becomes even less significant when you consider that many of these cheese imports are prepackaged and shipped in small packages ready for the retail market.
It is interesting to note that the reported facts in this particular case, according to the district supervisor for the Department of Agriculture, include the admission that although his department monitors all cheese imports to see that weights are labelled correctly and butterfat composition is up to standard, there is no monitoring of these products for freshness. Indeed no regulations exist governing the freshness of imported cheese products. The supervisor went on to comment that the department does not inspect every shipment that comes into the country, but rather it depends on the importer's record as to whether or not we take samples for inspection.
June 15, 1976

It is interesting to note as well that, according to comments from a spokesman from the health protection branch, when imported food comes into this country it is not checked by health inspectors for bacteria contamination unless there has been some complaint.
Regardless of the minister's answer to my question on May 25, and likely including the reply that I am about to receive tonight from his capable parliamentary secretary, one must remain convinced that under the present policy of the government our own Canadian cheese industry remains at a serious disadvantage right here at home in relation to foreign competitors.
In the case of Feta, Mr. Speaker, it wholesaled for $1.40 a pound compared to 90 cents to $1.29 for imports, and this particular shipment of 18,000 pounds was being offered by the importer at 50 to 60 cents a pound below market price if it could be cleaned up.
Cheese imports have been a bone of contention to the Canadian cheese manufacturing and Canadian dairy industries for some time. The present 50 million pounds of imports is estimated to be costing our own industry over $3.6 million.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that if the minister continues to refuse to reduce or place an embargo upon cheese imports, then I submit he is obligated at the very least to take immediate steps to place imported cheese under the same type of rigid inspection regulations that are currently applied to our Canadian producers. Anything less than this is totally unacceptable, grossly unfair, and highly dangerous to the health and well-being of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Irenes Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR EMBARGO ON IMPORTATION OF CHEESE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 25 an article appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail which was entitled "Mould Scraped Off Cheese". This article, by its implica-
Adjournment Debate
tions, may have caused concern to consumers. I am pleased to have the opportunity of touching briefly on the actual fact of this matter.
In late 1974 and early 1975, several shipments of Feta cheese from Denmark were imported in Toronto. This cheese was packed in barrels and covered with brine. Only the last shipment, dated March 10, 1975, brought difficulties; due to the evaporation of the brine, part of the cheese was no longer covered by the solution, which caused the growth of mould.

In an attempt to determine the best disposition of this product, some of the cheese was scraped clean of mould, rebrined, and repackaged. This reconditioned cheese was tested by the health protection branch and was found to be suitable for human consumption on the basis of analyses performed to date. Additional tests are currently being run to make absolutely sure that this assessment is correct. [Translation]
We got in touch with a Canadian manufacturer of Feta cheese to see whether he was interested in reconditioning a certain amount of cheese. This business is in direct competition with imported Feta cheese. The Health Protection Branch which was very careful in this matter has been retaining all the mouldy cheese since April 30.

The foregoing prompt action is illustrative of the effective control of both imported and domestic cheese which is exercised by the actions of the food inspection system of the Government of Canada. It would be unfortunate if erroneous impressions were gained, by situations such as this, that the food inspection system of Canada was not effective and efficient, since, indeed it is efficient.
